Arke Studio · first pass
Sample world invented to make the design honest: The Undersong, a coastal fantasy where a drowned god still sings beneath the harbour. Every image area is a live drop target: drag your own art onto any placeholder and it sticks. Chrome stays neutral monochrome (the design system's contract) so the creator's imagery carries all the colour. Motion: choreographed entrances, ambient drift on resting cards, tilt-to-straighten on hover. Below: the app’s screens in flow order (home → world → cast → sheet → canon → artifacts → productions → dispatch), followed by an archive of earlier explorations.
95The first thing said has to be said, and the captions under it go (found by driving the installed app; trims 89a, 91a, 91b, 91c)

Binding. Opening a conversation and speaking into it are two acts, and a screen that only does the first leaves the person unanswered. Typing a season brief into Production Chat cleared the composer and did nothing else: no conversation, no error, nothing on disk. Two faults sat on top of each other and each hid the other. The create frame caps a title at 200 characters and a frame that fails its schema is dropped without a word, so any opening longer than about two sentences vanished on the wire. Underneath that, creating a conversation does not take a turn — the screen created one with the message as its title and returned, so even a short opening became a label nothing ever answered. A title is derived from what was said, clipped at a word; what was said is sent. Day one hands its line to the chat rather than creating a thread nobody speaks into.

Binding. A caption that restates the screen is not reassurance, it is another thing to read. Gone: still soft · saying more changes them · wrap-up is what stages them under the points, which the panel’s own still a maybe and Save already say; nothing is settled yet · save a point above to make it ready under the wrap-up, which the disabled button already is; and this is the proposal · nothing above it has been written, which the accept’s own caption already names. Two of them were also false. The season page and the episode page each ended in a line beginning opening an episode opens its own chat — which turn 92 had made untrue three turns earlier, when a tile started opening the page. A caption nobody reads is also a caption nobody notices has gone stale.

Binding. What survives the trim is what a screen cannot show. talking changes nothing · wrap-up stages what you keep stays under every composer, because a person about to type a paragraph into somebody else’s software cannot see that it writes nothing, and nothing else on the screen says so. The accept’s caption stays too, because the gate writes season.json · nothing else moves names a consequence that has not happened yet. The test is not brevity: it is whether the line states something the screen is not already showing.

Found by driving the installed app, which is the only place either fault was visible: the suite was green, the types were sound, and every screen rendered. A conversation that opens and stays silent looks exactly like one waiting for you to say more.

94Scene Chat, and the pattern closes — three levels, one shape, built (completes 91; no new drawing, by 91’s own reasoning)

Binding. A scene is talked through in place, like everything above it. Its conversation opened World Chat, on another screen, which is where every production thread used to start and where turn 88 stopped sending people at the season. So a person who had learned the shape twice — talk here, accept here, land on the thing — found it stopped working at exactly the level where the writing happens, and the one that gets used most. Scene Chat is the same component with a smaller subject: the same transcript, the same two rail states, the same Accept Proposal, landing on the scene. No new drawing, which is turn 91’s own reasoning applied rather than repeated: a rail drawn once on 91b is a rail understood everywhere, and the only thing that changes is the subject in the eyebrow.

Binding. The scene page keeps Shots and Board, and they are not the same kind of thing as a tab elsewhere. One level up, a tab is the level below — Episodes under a season, Scenes under an episode. Here Shots is the level below and Board is a lens on it, priced and ordered, which turn 53 settled as the only surface a scene is spent from. Two entries, so it stays a strip rather than becoming a heading, and it is left alone: the thing this turn changes is where the conversation opens, not what the scene screen shows.

Binding. A rail item owns the screens reached by drilling into it. Season owns an episode’s two screens, and Scenes owns a scene’s, because neither lives under the path its rail item points at — a chat lives under story/, beside the production’s own. Without this the rail goes blank at exactly the moment somebody is two levels deep and most wants to know where they are. Stated as a rule here because it has now been fixed twice and will be needed again the first time anything else grows a level.

The shape is built at all three levels and nothing is left of the list this run started from. What is still not done, and is the one thing the pattern still promises without delivering: turn 87’s cascade — an episode’s own proposal creating the scenes it needs, rather than scenes drafted elsewhere and adopted from a pool. Every screen now says out loud that the arrow runs backwards there. That is a change to what wrap-up stages, not to any screen, and it is its own turn.

93An episodic production’s front page is its season, and a production with a season is not on day one (folds the Dashboard for one medium; fixes what 53b’s check counted)

Binding. A production that has a season is not on day one. The check for an empty production counted scenes, takes and chapters — three things a microdrama can be a long way into a season without having. So a season with a question, an ending and three written episodes still opened on “Nothing written yet. Say what happens…”, offering Shape the whole thing first to somebody who had just finished doing exactly that, while the Season screen next door said 3 written. Two screens in one production contradicting each other about whether it has been started, and the day-one one was wrong. What makes a production started is anything the gate has written to it, which for an episodic one is its season and its episodes before it is ever a scene.

Binding. An episodic production’s front page is its season. Turn 91 settled that a production is exactly one season; if that is true then the production’s own address and the season’s are the same address, and keeping them apart is what produced the contradiction above. The rail’s first item is Season and there is no second entry for it. Day one needs no screen of its own here either: a Microdrama is created saying how many episodes it has, so its empty state is already drawn — 91a with every tile dashed, which is turn 87’s rule that the shape of a season is a thing to see before it is a thing to fill. What an empty season adds is one line naming where it gets shaped, because a board of dashed tiles says what is missing and not what to do about it.

Binding. What the fold costs is said, not hidden. An episodic production loses the dashboard’s awaiting review card and its next uncovered shot from its front page. That is a real loss and it is a small one: both are shot-level, both live on Generate, and the rail already carries the count beside Generate’s name. It is also the wrong altitude for this screen — a season’s own “what next” is which episode is unwritten, which the board states in tiles. The dashboard is unchanged for every other medium: a Story production keeps 54a, a one-off Video keeps its own, and neither has a season for its front page to be.

Still open, carried from 92: the scene is the old screen — tabs for Shots and Board, no conversation, no accept — so the shape repeats three times in the drawing and twice in the build. That is the last level, and the one that makes the pattern a pattern rather than a coincidence.

92Three things found by walking it: the season had no accept, a press that staged an episode said nothing, and one tile went two places (applies 91 where it was missing; amends 91a in place)

Binding. Every level has a wrap-up and an accept, and the season is a level. Turn 91 bound the pattern and drew it one level down, on 91b, on the reasoning that a rail drawn once is a rail understood everywhere. The build then took that literally: the episode got a wrap-up and an Accept Proposal, and Production Chat was left with a link to Season and nothing else — no way to stage what had been said, no way to accept it, no landing. So the one hop everybody walks first, decide the season and arrive at it, was the single place in the whole workspace where the pattern did not exist. A pattern with a hole at its entrance is not a pattern. Production Chat carries the wrap-up 89a already draws and the second rail state 91b already draws, against season.json — or story.json for a production with no season — and accepting lands on Season, or on Overview.

Binding. A control that stages something says so where it was pressed. Pressing a blank episode tile staged the episode exactly as intended and changed nothing on the screen: the only mark anywhere was an unlabelled dot in the far corner of the chrome, three hundred pixels from the press and attached to a different subject. That is the same failure as a message sent into a screen that keeps no trace of it — the work happened, and the person has no way to know, so they press again, or conclude it is broken. The tile becomes the staged tile, carrying the name the proposal gave it and marked as waiting, and it stays that way until the gate writes it. Feedback belongs at the point of the press; a counter somewhere else is a receipt filed in another room.

Binding. One control, one destination. An episode tile opened the episode’s chat when nothing was written and its page when something was. That reads as thoughtful and is the opposite: the same click lands in two different places according to state a person cannot see before clicking, so the only way to learn where a tile goes is to press it and find out. A tile always opens its page. An empty page that says nothing is written yet and offers one way into the thread is exactly what day one already is a level up — 53b is a page with a composer on it, not a redirect into a conversation — and the rule it follows is the older one: a screen is an address, and an address does not move.

Found by walking the built thing rather than by reading it, which is the only reason any of the three is here. Still open, and named so the next turn does not have to rediscover them: Dashboard and Season both answer “what is this thing” for an episodic production, and one of them should go; and the scene is still the old screen — tabs for Shots and Board, no conversation, no accept — so the shape turn 91 repeats three times is a shape the build keeps twice.

91A production is one season, and one shape repeats all the way down (collapses 88’s pair into a pattern; amends 89’s two rails and 48’s tab strip; supersedes 53c)

Binding. A production is exactly one season, and another season is another production. Nothing was ever built to hold a second one — no switcher, no picker, no address that names which season is meant — and the word nevertheless appeared everywhere as though a choice were coming. It cost a whole tab: a Season view whose job was to show which season you were in, on a screen that could only ever show one. What the season is now lives in the page’s own header — the question it answers, how it ends, its counts, and the Series engine it inherits, read-only as turn 48 settled. A view you always land on is not a tab, and a tab strip of one item is a heading wearing a border. This applies to the episode page too (91c): an episode has exactly one plural child, so Scenes is drawn as a heading and gains a strip on the day it gains a sibling — the structure the level below is reached through is the point, not the chrome it is reached through.

Binding. Every level is the same two screens: a chat that ends in an accept, and a page whose children are its tab. Production Chat settles the season and lands on the season page, whose tabs are Episodes and Arcs. An episode’s tile opens Episode Chat, which lands on the episode page, whose tab is Scenes. A scene opens Scene Chat, which lands on the scene page, whose tab is its shots. Three levels, one shape, learned once. This is why 53c is superseded rather than amended: it drew an episode as a conversation and a promise editor sharing a surface, which is the exact half-and-half screen turn 88 broke apart one level up, and it is broken apart here for the same reason.

Binding. The rail beside a conversation has two states, and never both at once. While talking it is turn 89’s points: soft, one sentence each, changed by saying more. At the end it is the staged proposal — every field with what it was and what it would become — under one action, Accept Proposal. Turn 89 forbade showing thinking and a decision together and that rule is kept exactly; what it wrongly implied is that the two must live on different screens. They must live at different times. “Turn this into a proposal” is retired everywhere it appears: by the time a person is reading what the conversation settled, it already is one, and a button that converts a noun into another noun names an implementation step rather than a decision a person is making.

Binding. Accepting lands you on the thing you accepted, and that thing can always be talked to again. An accept is not the end of a subject — you will come back and say more about the same episode next week — so a page reached by accepting must carry one way back into its own thread, and exactly one. Without it the accept is a one-way door and the second conversation has nowhere to start. This is also what makes the pattern navigable in both directions: down through a tab, back up through a link that names the level above.

Binding. Direction loses its tab and keeps its field. Nobody has yet been able to say what Direction decides that the world’s look and a scene’s own description do not, and a tab that cannot be explained is a tab that will be filled in wrongly. The field stays on the season record and the conversation may still settle it; there is simply no screen insisting on it until there is a reason. This is turn 53’s rule applied to something already drawn: build the plain version, and add to it only once the plain version has been used and found wanting.

Following from this: the episodes grid keeps its dashed tiles from turn 87 and loses the conversation at its foot that 45b drew, because the chat is now a level above it. Scene Chat and the scene page are the same two screens again with a smaller subject and want no new drawing beyond 49a’s script and 53e’s board. Turn 87’s cascade is what fills the rail on 91b: the five scenes an episode needs are part of the episode’s own proposal, not adopted afterwards from a pool. The scene frames are not redrawn here and still print the retired wording — 49a, 49b and 53e all say Turn this into a proposal — and they are superseded on that one word and nothing else, because redrawing three drawings to change a button is a worse trade than saying so.

89Production Chat — the same thing as World Chat, one scope down, and it shows what it understood (renames 78’s Development; corrects 88’s bare chat)

Binding. The rail item is Production Chat. “Development” named a phase of filmmaking rather than a thing on a screen, so it told a person when they were rather than what this is; turn 78 renamed it once already and the word was the problem both times. This screen is World Chat with a production for a subject — the same transcript, the same points, the same wrap-up, the same gate — and naming it so teaches the whole model in two words: a person who has used one knows what this is before opening it. The route keeps its name; a rename is display, never wiring.

Binding. A conversation shows what it understood, as it understands it. Turn 88 took the staged-proposal rail off the chat, correctly — that belongs with the details, where the object is — but left the chat with nothing beside it, and a conversation whose understanding is invisible until wrap-up asks a person to talk for ten minutes on faith. World Chat has answered this since #70: points, grouped by the subject each is about, one sentence each, marked settled or still open. Production Chat carries the same panel, and its subjects are the production’s own — the season question, its ending, each episode, each arc, the direction — so a season being broken into episodes is watched happening rather than discovered afterwards.

Binding. The two rails are different things and must not be confused for one. Beside a conversation: what it currently understands, still soft, editable by saying more. Beside a details screen: what is staged against the object and waiting on a yes. One is thinking, the other is a decision at the door. A screen showing both would be claiming a point is a proposal, which is the exact promise the gate exists to keep.

Binding. The sweep is part of the rename, and it stops at display. Every frame’s rail now reads Production Chat, the way turn 78 swept its own; a drawing left saying the old word is a drawing that will be believed. What does not move is the domain: the development.* change classifications (SPEC-023 R-20) are persisted identifiers on records already written, and renaming those is a migration rather than a rename. The prose of earlier turns stays as written too — a turn is a record of what was decided when, and editing it to agree with a later decision destroys the only thing it is for.

Following from this: an episode’s chat and a scene’s chat are the same screen with a smaller subject (R-20’s other two context kinds), so they are Episode Chat and Scene Chat and want no new drawing beyond their subjects. The points panel is also where turn 87’s cascade becomes visible: scenes an episode needs appear as points before they are ever files.

88Talking and looking stop sharing a screen — Development is the conversation, Season is what it made (amends 48’s one tab strip; keeps its layout rule for the views; applies 86)

Binding. One conversation, on its own screen, and the details on another. Turn 48 gave the workspace four views and hung a conversation on each, so one thread — SPEC-023 R-20 says there is only ever one per production — wore four costumes, and every screen was half a place to make something and half a place to read it. A person could not tell which they were doing. Development is now the conversation and nothing else: full width, no draft rail, the thread that sets up the foundations. Season is the details — the season record and its views, Episodes, Arcs and Direction — where what the conversation produced is read and worked with. Two rail items, because they are two things a person does.

Binding. Turn 48’s layout rule survives, one level down. It governed where a conversation sat; with the conversation gone from these views it governs the views alone, unchanged in substance: Season and Direction each show one object and keep the 470px rail beside what is staged against it; Episodes and Arcs are comparisons across the season and take the full surface. A non-episodic production has no season, so its details screen is the overview and the rail names it that; there is no season tab standing empty for a short film (turn 83).

Binding. What one conversation produced is reviewed as one thing. A setup conversation that settles the season question, its ending, its episodes and its direction stages them together and they are accepted together — R-20’s batched wrap-up, now stated as a rule about what a person sees rather than only about how the gate is fed. Splitting them into four proposals asks somebody to re-decide, one file at a time, what they just decided once in sentences.

Open, and the same question one level down: an episode and a scene each have a conversation and a detail view too (R-20’s other two context kinds), so this split either repeats there or it is not a model. Drawing them is the next turn’s work, together with turn 87’s dashed board and the cascade that fills it.

87How a season becomes scenes — the board shows its shape from the start, and an episode’s conversation makes the scenes it needs (applies 45, 53 and 86; follows SPEC-023 R-20)

Binding. An episodic board shows the season it was promised, from the moment the season exists. A Microdrama is created saying how many episodes it has; the board draws that many tiles immediately, dashed and empty until written, because the shape of the season is a thing to see before it is a thing to fill. The build hid the whole Episodes view until an episode already existed, so the one place named Episodes was invisible exactly when somebody was looking for where to make one — and creation lived on the Season tab, a different subject. Making an episode happens in the grid (45b): a dashed tile is started by opening it, and the last tile adds one beyond the declared count. No screen asks for a title before there is anything to title.

Binding. One conversation per thing being decided, at three levels. SPEC-023 R-20’s context kinds are the shape: the production thread holds the season — its question, its ending, the board, the arcs, the direction; an episode has its own thread; a scene has its own. A conversation about one episode does not drag the whole season through it, and the board’s own composer stays with the production thread because “episode 5 needs a reason to exist” is an observation across the season and not about episode 5 alone.

Binding. An episode’s wrap-up stages the scenes it needs, not only its promise. This is the cascade the model has been missing: talking through an episode produces its promise and the scenes in order, staged together and accepted at the gate like everything else. Scenes stop arriving only by being drafted elsewhere and adopted from a pool of unassigned ones — adoption stays, because a scene that already exists must still be able to find its episode, but it is the exception rather than the only road. A scene so staged carries no shots: accepting a scene creates shots and dispatches nothing (49a) is unchanged.

The order this wants building: the dashed board and creation-in-the-grid first, because it fixes finding the place at all; then the per-episode thread; then the cascade, which is the piece that changes what wrap-up stages. Arcs necessarily follows episodes — a lane cites the episode its setup, turn and payoff land in, so it has nowhere to land until they exist.

86Development authors through its conversation, and the field editors are retired (applies 44 and 48; amends nothing drawn — the frames already say this and the build had answered differently)

Binding. One way to author a season, and it is the conversation. The build grew a second: a form editor behind Start the season, Edit the direction and Propose overview, sitting beside a Talk it through button that opened the thread on another screen. Two ways into one file is how a person ends up asking what the conversation is for — and the answer, that it reads the world and drafts against it while a form cannot, is not visible from a screen offering both. The field editors are removed. What a person types goes to the production’s own thread (44, SPEC-023 R-20), and the thread is the only path to season.json.

Binding. The conversation is in the view, not on another screen. Turn 48’s layout rule decides where: Season, Direction and the non-episodic overview each author one object, so the transcript and its composer hold the left column and the 470px rail carries the draft; Episodes and Arcs are comparisons, so they keep the surface and the conversation becomes a row at the foot. The transcript and composer are one surface shared with World Chat rather than a second rendering of the same turns, because two drawings of one conversation drift the moment either is touched.

Binding. The rail shows what is staged, marked on the field it would change, with the accepted text beneath. It is derived from the staged proposal’s own field-by-field review — never a second copy of the draft kept beside it — so what the screen promises and what the gate would write cannot disagree. A view with nothing staged shows the accepted object and says so plainly; a view with nothing accepted says that instead, in words, and never as a greyed control.

Unchanged and still true: talking writes nothing, wrap-up stages, acceptance stays in the gate. Left for its own turn: the episode screen’s promise editor (53c) is the same shape of question one level down, and the scene script (49a) is a third; neither is decided here.

85Step one’s words are settled from the build, and both creation steps are made real (amends 43’s step-one copy; applies 83 and 53; follows 84’s third card)

Binding. Frame 43a’s step-one copy is retired in favour of the built copy. Two drawings of one screen disagreed: 6a named what each family is (“Prose and scripts, drafted inside the canon with the world as editor”), 43a compressed it to what each family produces (“Prose in chapters, ordered and versioned”). The built screen carries 6a’s, it has been read by people who then made things, and it is the copy that survived turn 84’s replacement of the third card. It is now the approved copy, and 43a is read for its structure only — the modal over the world’s key art, the name field, the joins line, and the caption beneath the buttons. The third card reads Interactive video, never Stills: Stills is a lens on Generate and is not a family anything is created as.

Binding. The caption under step one’s buttons is not decoration. nothing generates · nothing is copied out of the world is the promise that the primary action spends nothing and takes nothing out of the world, said where the finger already is. A step one without it makes a person learn that by pressing.

Binding. Every default 53a draws is asked, episode length included. A Microdrama is a Microdrama because of how long its episodes run, so the range belongs to the person creating one and not to a constant: it is chosen on step two and written into season.json, where Development shows it back. The three kinds are all offered — Short film, Music video, Microdrama series — because a kind only sets starting numbers, and a Video production is the same scenes, shots, takes and cut whichever is picked. Music video is therefore offered before turn 60’s Spine exists; what it lacks is authoring, not coherence.

The kind cards hold a banner area they have no art for, so the choice is still made by reading. Three images are wanted — short film, music video, Microdrama — and the layout is already sized for them. Also open from this pass: 43a’s day-one companion is still frame 43b in the app, which turn 83 superseded in whole.

84The retired game screens get their dispositions in one pass — Interactive video’s surfaces bind to its accepted brief (applies the revised Scope §11; follows the Interactive-video brief rev 1; amends nothing drawn — a decision turn, like 78)

Binding. The §11 dispositions apply as one pass, never piecemeal. 34a and 34b are replaced (the picker’s third card is Interactive video; day one becomes start scene plus first choice). 34c, 34d, 34e and 34j are reassigned (branch summary, dashboard reusables, the branch map, route preview with edge traversal). 34f is removed and nothing replaces it — the schema is the removal. 34g is replaced by the named-findings panel. 34h and 34i are kept. 35a is removed initially and 35b–35e hold with deferred Interact. Until a screen’s replacement is drawn, the retired frame keeps its old chrome as dated record.

Binding. The branch map is Interactive video’s structural authority and nobody else’s. Deterministic layered layout — longest-path layers from the start scene, in-layer order by authored choice order then id — so the same graph always draws the same picture. Start ringed, endings flagged, exclusions dimmed with their reason, reconvergence as edges joining an existing node, never a duplicate. Every node and edge keyboard-reachable in layout order. A linear season never shows this map (turn 78 stands).

Binding. Findings are named, with evidence, and never a number. The findings panel lists each finding in the brief’s vocabulary — the scene, the choice, the route it names — and marks which block publication and which warn. No percentage, no health score, no aggregate grade appears anywhere in the medium; drawing one is how 34g comes back.

Asset note: the picker needs a new Interactive-video banner (ms-interact.png stays held with deferred Interact); ms-watch.png and ms-choose.png keep. The drawn frames for the branch map, findings panel, day one and player arrive with epic 401’s client issues, each against this turn’s bindings and the brief’s sections 3–5.

83Two reconciliations after the domain settles — episodic ownership is qualified, and step one stops skipping step two (amends 78; supersedes turn 43’s day-one seed rule in whole; follows SPEC-023, the accepted narrative-domain specification)

Binding. Episode ownership is a property of episodic productions, not of every production. Turn 78’s fourth rule stands where episodes exist and is now qualified the way SPEC-023 R-11 decides it: an episodic production — a Microdrama or a series — requires every scene to belong to exactly one episode, with a boundary-crossing moment written as two linked scenes; a non-episodic film has no episodes at all and draws no episode surfaces — three tabs, never four greyed (turn 48). Interactive video’s release grouping is settled by its own brief, and no screen here presumes it either way.

Binding. A family with more than one kind cannot create from step one. With such a family selected, step one’s primary action continues to step two and says so — it does not create; the kind and the numbers that differ between kinds (turn 53) are chosen before anything exists. Where the selected family has one kind, step one’s action creates directly and step two never renders — turn 47’s toll rule, now stated from both sides. Applied to the Prototype’s live path: frame 6a’s primary — drawn with Video selected — now reads Continue · what kind of video? and routes to step two instead of creating past it.

Binding. The day-one seed rule is superseded in whole. Turn 43 bound two seed sources on day one; turn 53 cut the seed rails, and an empty production is a place to start writing, not a briefing. Seeds return only when the plain path has been used and found wanting — and if they do, they return as a new turn, not by reviving 43’s rule. The brief’s Programme A item and SPEC-012 R-3 now record the same disposition; issue 386 closed as superseded.

A decision turn with no frames, like turn 78: the qualified rule and the create-path rule change wiring and words, not drawings — redrawing 6a for one button is the two-drawings drift. The domain wording lives in SPEC-023 (medium, kind, Series at series/<slug>.json, season beside its production, episodes with stable stems and explicit order); this document binds what screens show and the Prototype walks.

Binding. The rail folds to marks; it does not go away. 44 wide, icons only, exactly the destination rail the bench already uses — every place the production rail reached stays one click away, and only the words are spent. The 300 the labels were using becomes the artifact panel, so the cut itself loses no width at all.

Binding. Placement is authored, and authored placement lives on its own lane. This amends 79’s third binding, which said nothing on the cut is placed by drag. The V lane still refuses it: a shot sits where the story put it or where the song does, and dragging one would be a second answer to a question that already has one. What a drop makes is an overlay — an artifact at a time you chose — on its own OV lane, stored in cut.json beside the audio placement that file already holds. Two lanes, two rules, and still one answer to where a shot sits.

Binding. An overlay is not a take and never becomes one. It cites an artifact by id and carries no provenance, no canon revision, no cost and no review. It cannot be accepted, because nothing about it was dispatched or judged — the gate is for authored facts and for generated work, and a plate laid over the picture is neither. Deleting it removes the placement and never the artifact.

Binding. An overlay that does not reach the export is decoration. It renders over the picture for its own window and changes nothing outside it, so a cut watched here and a cut exported are the same film. Where it covers a gap it covers a slate, not a shot — an overlay is never coverage, and the footer counts it separately: 13 of 15 shots covered · 1 overlay.

Binding. Bands. Scene band 16, V lane 58, OV lane 44, A lane 30, selected-shot strip 46, 6 between rows, lane label 24 now that one is two characters. The overlay lane is deliberately shorter than the picture: it is not the film, it is what is laid over it, and a lane of equal weight would read as a second cut.

Three things this turn does not settle. Two overlays covering the same second need an order, and nothing here says which wins. Whether an overlay can be trimmed — it has a window, so the question is real — is left to the turn that draws its own strip. And the export is bound above but not drawn: compositing a plate over the picture is an ffmpeg filter graph this design has never asked for, and it wants its own accounting before anyone promises a date.

Binding. The lane is one cell per shot, under a band of scenes. 24a merged a scene's covered shots into a single cell, which reads well and makes the only editable thing unselectable — a scene is not a clip and never was. The scene keeps its grouping in the band, exactly as the song's sections do in 80a, and the lane carries the unit of work. Gaps keep 24a's two cards unchanged: shot 14 in amber where its scene has other coverage, scene 5, no takes yet in neutral where it has none.

Binding. On this clock the strip states the slot, not a budget. A shot's authored duration is its place in the film — shot 4.0s — and beside it the material that has to fill it, take 6.0s. Trim moves the in-point inside that material and never moves the slot. This is the one line where the two strips differ: 80a's budget is a window on the track, and a window is something the song fixed; a slot is something the story authored.

Binding. A trim that leaves nothing is the gap the screen already draws. Not a new state, not an error, and not a silently blank shot: the shot becomes an ordinary gap card, and the export slates it the way it slates every other gap (R-15, R-20). The same is true on the song clock, where it becomes a slate — one rule, two vocabularies, and no third thing to learn.

Binding. Both clocks share one set of bands. Scene or section band 16, V lane 58, A lane 30, selected-shot strip 46, 6 between rows, and flex weights of seconds × 10. The Cut is one screen reading two clocks (79), so switching between a short film and a music video must not move a single row.

Two corrections and one gap. 24a's footer read 30s uncovered against its own cells — 0:22 + 0:38 + 0:30 + 0:13 is 1:43 of a 2:40 film, so 57s is uncovered; corrected in place, and 81a's fifteen shots sum to the same 160s. The gap is real and not drawn: on this clock a clip contributes its own length to the export, not the shot's authored duration, so a 6.0s take in a 4.0s slot exports six seconds and trimming 1.5s exports four and a half. Whether the slot should bound the clip is a decision this turn does not take.

Binding. One Cut, two clocks. The Cut tab is a single surface whose clock is the story when the production has no spine and the song when it has one; deriveCut and deriveSpineCut are two readings of one screen, never two screens. Spine (60a) stays an authoring surface — it is where a shot is anchored to the track — and never renders a second cut. Today CutScreen calls deriveCut unconditionally while Exports picks by spine, so a music video’s Cut tab and its Exports screen state different films; closing that is what this turn is for.

Binding. Uncovered time is black, and a black states its length. On the song clock every moment from 0 to the track’s measured end is a segment, so what no anchor claims is drawn as black at its true width with its duration on it — 17.6s, 1:42.0. A black is never closed by moving a neighbouring clip, and the footer counts them the way 24a counts gaps: 3 blacks · 2:27 uncovered. Story-clock productions keep 24a’s dashed gap cards; the two vocabularies are not merged, because a shot with no take and time no shot claims are different facts.

Binding. Trim is the only authored edit the Cut offers, and it trims from the in-point. It writes trimInSec on the selection — not on the take, which is immutable, and not on the anchor, which is the window — and it resets to 0 when the accepted take changes. There is no reorder, no drag, no split and no razor on either clock: the cut follows the story, not drag order. Long material is trimmed from trimInSec; short material plays and then holds a labelled slate; nothing is stretched, frozen or looped.

Binding. Bands, on the timeline block. Section band 16, V lane 58, A lane 30, selected-clip strip 46, with 6 between rows. Every row on the song clock shares one scale — flex weights are seconds × 10 against a 222.140s track — so a section band, a clip and a black at the same moment align by construction rather than by eye.

Three things named and not drawn. The sample anchors on 60a sum to 1:14.5 covered against its own printed budgets, so its 2:14 was the single figure on that screen disagreeing with the rest; corrected in place to 1:14, which is what 80a carries. No frame writes trimInSec: the field, the derivation and the reset all exist, so the gap is one message wide. And the play control is drawn live here but ships pointer-events:none, which is the difference between a cut you can review and a picture of one.

Binding. The notification is an Activity row, arriving early. Dot, then the target named target-then-kind (Scene 11, 4 shots), then one mono line of figures — the bands 26a already uses for a job, at the same 10.5px and the same --neutral-400. Open Activity and the row must say the same words; two spellings of one job is how a queue stops being believable.

Binding. The title says what happened; the second line says what it costs. The state is one word at the end of the title — queued, running, ready, failed — because a notification that names a thing and some figures never states its own purpose: read cold, Shot 2, clip over Seedance 2.0 · ~$1.82 could be a status readout rather than a receipt. The verb costs one word and replaces the count the figures line used to carry, so the notification gets shorter. The second line is model · cost, plus · N ahead only when something the user did not just dispatch is actually in front of it — the rest of its own batch is one press, not a queue. A local run reads local where the figure would be, because there is nothing to spend. The path is not repeated. The user pressed the button on the surface that owns the work, so The Undersong · Bell Watch · ep 3 is telling them where they are standing — the title localises it, and Activity holds the rest. A tilde marks an estimate (~$5.46, as 68c has it); a bare figure is money already spent.

Binding. Queued is not success. Accepted work carries the plain border and the foreground dot. The success green belongs to a job that came back (79g) and to nothing else — green on an enqueue tells a person their shot is ready when nothing has run yet.

Binding. One job, one notification, updated in place. The row that said queued becomes the row that says running and then the row that came back, carrying the same id — a second notification never arrives to contradict the first. At most three on screen at once; the rest wait, because Activity holds all of it anyway.

Binding. A refusal earns a third line; nothing else does. It carries the provider’s own words and then what became of the work: FAL rejected the key (HTTP 401). 4 shots held. The cause a person can act on, and whether they must ask again. Couldn’t add this to Activity gives neither. This is the one band allowed to wrap.

Binding. The action names where the fix is, not always Activity. A rejected key sends the user to Providers; work that came back offers View; work that never queued gets no action at all, because Activity would be an empty screen. This generalises the inActivity: false case the client already has for uploads.

Binding. Bands, not a total. Width 390, padding 14px 16px, dot 7 at margin-top:6 (thumbnail 36 when a picture came back), title 600 13px and the mono line 10.5/1.45 set 3px below — both clipped with an ellipsis, never wrapped — and the reason, when there is one, 11px/1.5 set var(--space-2) below. Right group is the action at 30px tall — its width follows its label — then a 16 close, var(--space-2) apart, at margin-top:2 so it sits on the title. Placed top-centre at 44px + var(--space-3), on var(--card) at var(--radius-card) with var(--shadow-lg) — it floats over a working screen, so it needs more separation than a pill.

Try next: "the notification for a proposal, which is not a job and has no estimate" · "a dispatch refused before the queue — 72f’s pinned-file mismatch said this way"

78The workspace takes its production name — Story stays a family in the picker, Development is the layer inside every production (renames the rail item across every production screen here and in the Prototype; amends 44, 45, 47, 48, 53; follows the revised Vision and Scope, and revision 5 of the brief)

Binding. The rail item reads Development; the picker card keeps Story. Story names a production family in the create dialog — novels, scripts, written work — and Development names the narrative-development layer inside every production, whatever its family: one word doing both jobs is how a picker and a tab end up claiming each other. The workflow reads Development → Production → Release. Applied as a sweep, not a redraw: the label changed in place on every drawn production screen of the surviving families in this document and in the Prototype — the retired game screens (34a–35e) keep their old chrome until their scope-cleanup disposition — and the Prototype’s wiring — go.story, the story screen name — is unchanged, because a display rename that edits three wiring sites per tab is how a prototype breaks. Turn 48’s four views, its tab strip and every number it binds stand unchanged under the new name.

Binding. Microdrama is one word wherever a screen writes it — the kind card, its banner placeholder, the step-two label. The Vision names the format; a screen does not respell it. Earlier turns’ rule prose keeps the spelling it was written with, as dated record.

Binding. A linear season never shows a branch map. The season board is the only structural view of a Video production, and explicit order is its only authority. Branching belongs to Interactive video — the Scope reassigns the old chapter graph, frame 34e, as its branch map, with direct routing only: a choice selects the next scene, and there are no variables, no conditions, no unlocks, no hidden state, and no score; structural checks report named findings. Nothing in this document’s turns draws any of that, so nothing here had to be removed.

Binding. An episode card owns whole scenes. Every scene belongs to exactly one episode; a dramatic moment that crosses a release boundary is written as two linked scenes — a closing and an opening — and no board draws one scene split across two episode cards. Sample copy on the season board and the episode screen must satisfy this, and does.

Nothing else moved: 47a’s action already reads Create Series and open day one and 48a already shows the Series engine as a read-only card, which is the thin Series the brief records as decided. The Prototype’s game screens (34a–35e) keep their old chrome untouched: the Scope’s cleanup table assigns each a disposition, and they move when Interactive video gets its own brief, as one pass rather than piecemeal. The Vision and Scope live with the product documents, beside the repository rather than in it.

Binding. A voice recipe is not a new surface. It is a row in the list 75b already draws, on the engine 75b already describes, and the header simply gains a third capability. Local cloned voice asks the user to install nothing they were not already asked for — which is the entire reason it runs here rather than in a runtime of our own, and would be undone by giving it a screen of its own.

Binding. A refused recipe names both figures and what still works. Needs 8 GB VRAM. This machine has 4 GB. is the measured floor against the measured machine, and Cloud voice still works via ElevenLabs. is the alternative the same capability has. This is 72's vocabulary applied unchanged: the row is disabled, never hidden, and never reads a bare "unavailable".

Binding. A drifted node is stated as a version, not as absence. TTS-Audio-Suite is at 4f8792f; this recipe was authored against dedd982. The node is present and answering — saying it is missing would send the user to reinstall something they already have. This is the first recipe with a custom node at all, so it is the first row that can refuse this way.

The recipe dispatches, and on this machine it does not finish. Re-measured through ComfyUI on 2026-08-19: the sampler is fast — 25 steps in 1s — and the stage after it runs out of card. Peak 9.35 GB and still climbing when it was killed, with 3.36 GB already taken by other applications before Arke asked for anything. The 5.44 GB in SPEC-022 was a true measurement of the model on a Python harness and a false statement of what the recipe needs, so the floor is now 8 GB and the gate’s comparison against total VRAM is recorded as the deeper bug. The clone flow itself is verified end to end in the installed app: clip staged, uploaded byte-identical, graph accepted, voice written to the library. Two gaps remain deliberate and are not drawn here because nothing in this turn depends on them — the recipe pins no checkpoint digests, and the custom node is not vendored (D11).

Binding. This screen does not theme. The plate is always the dark one, so every value on it comes from the neutral ramp (--neutral-50, --neutral-400) or a literal, never from --foreground/--background — those invert under .dark and would erase the text in light mode. The host must also push the dark titlebar overlay for this screen whatever the user's theme preference (color:#0A0A0A, symbolColor:#FAFAFA), or the caption buttons vanish into the sky. The plate carries the only colour on the screen. Every card, button, icon and label is neutral; the warm horizon and flare live in the image, which is the design system's standing contract rather than an exception to it. The horizon must clear the cards. The plate puts it at 86% of frame height (731 of 850); the card row runs 270–652, leaving 79px. The plate anchors right, never centred. It is 3840×1522 (2.52:1) against a window that runs 1.6:1 to 2.33:1, so cover crops up to 1405px of source width; centred, the sun is driven to 99.5% and jams against the right edge. At 100% 50% it sits at 87% of the visible box, where the approved composition puts it, and only dark sky is lost from the left. Measured across the range: 1.60 → sun 87.0%, horizon 86.0%; 1.78 → 88.3%/85.8%; 2.33 → 91.3%/85.6%. The horizon is the footer’s rule. Nothing is drawn above the footer row: the plate’s own lit horizon separates the cards from the four links, and a hairline 18px beneath it is swallowed by the glow. Card bands: frame 382, icon 61, heading 28, description 45 (2 lines at 13.5/1.65), action 52, footnote 17. The lockup is measured, not eyeballed. Inside a 940 box the wordmark sets at 58px/.55em to 675 wide and the tagline at 16px/.83em to 619; the bar sits on the wordmark baseline and the flare centres at 81.4% of that box, which is the final O. Exactly one filled action. Launch Arke Studio is --neutral-900 on --neutral-50; every other control on the screen is outlined or plain. Cloud is named, not offered. Until the service exists the action reads Coming soon and is disabled — the card dims but is never removed, because the choice is the point of the screen. The screen remembers nothing. There is no skip-next-time; every launch asks. The four footer items have no destinations yet and are drawn inert; they must not ship as live controls that do nothing.

Open: the wordmark is set in Jost 200 at .55em tracking, a face the app does not load today — the shipped set is Geist and Geist Mono. Adopting it costs one more webfont for one string; the alternative is Geist Light, which will not match these letterforms. 76b is a proposal rather than a decision: it holds the plate under the setup panel drawn at 15a so the launch reads as one continuous surface, and the other route is a deliberate fade from this plate to the white setup page. The horizon is pinned to 86% of the viewport, not to a fixed offset, and the card row is centred; that holds the clearance from the 640px minimum height up to a maximised display. The plate ships as WebP at 0.89 MB (q98, 50.7 dB against the source) rather than the 6 MB PNG.

Binding. Local runtime is master and detail, built from 40a’s parts at 40a’s numbers: a 196px rail with a 14px gutter and a 1px rule, a detail pane at padding-left:22px, the body 624px tall. The rail is the heading — the pane carries no section eyebrow above the detail’s own, because the flat version had grown to nine eyebrows in one scroll and the rail is what replaces them. Every component is named once: the section that owns a thing states it, and a thing that has not arrived stays under Components, which is where Download, Skip and Retry live. A component whose owning section cannot speak — local models before detection returns — stays under Components rather than disappearing from both. Provider tools are never here: Higgsfield is a credential, and Providers owns it. A status is a dot leading its word at gap:6px, never a bare dot ending a row at the row’s own 12px, and never against the scroll edge. Actions attach to what they act on: a path is changed on the field that shows it, and no section carries more than three loose links — the voice section had seven. A band with nothing to state carries its actions and no value: the mapped ComfyUI models folder is a setting the coordinator does not publish on ComfyUiEngineStatus, so MODELS FOLDER offers the two actions and draws no path until modelsDir reaches the wire.

The rail groups are the sections that exist today, so nothing new is measured or fetched to draw this. Local runtime is the last settings pane that scrolls as a whole; with the detail capped the way .fy-prov caps its models list, the panel stops scrolling anywhere. Not covered: whether This machine earns a rail row or belongs in the panel’s subtitle, and where a second ComfyUI install would go if one were ever adopted.

Binding. The clip belongs to the voice, not to the take. 70e removed both reference lanes from voice mode because a text-to-speech route carries neither, and that stands: the composer in voice mode still offers no references and no keyframes. A cloned voice's recording is not a reference a shot cites — it is the voice's identity, chosen once when the voice is made and never again at generate time. It follows that the clip is not budgeted, not counted against referenceImages, and never appears on the bench.

Binding. A cloned voice belongs to the world, not to the character it was made for. The catalogue is ranked against a sheet but assembled independently of one, so a voice cloned while casting Maren is offered for every character afterwards — available to every character in this world. The recording still files as an artifact recording where it came from, which is provenance, not ownership. Assignment remains a sheet change, exactly as 70c requires.

Binding. The description is data, not decoration. A cloned clip arrives with no provider metadata, and rankVoices ranks a candidate with no attributes last — so a voice cloned for a character would sink below every preset when ranked against that same character. The description field is the fix and is therefore required: its words are lexically extracted into the attributes the picker matches. The screen states what it is for as data on the label (ranked against written voice), never as a sentence.

Binding. IndexTTS ships with no voices, and the empty source says so with a count. Every other source arrives populated — Kokoro with six presets, ElevenLabs with the account's library — and this one is empty until somebody clones something. The header count reads no voices and Assign is disabled; there is no illustration and no explanatory sentence. This is the only catalogue state in the app where the source is working correctly and still lists nothing.

Binding. Consent is a checkbox, not a paragraph. The model cannot tell whether the speaker in a clip agreed to be cloned, and neither can the app. One line, one required tick, on the screen where the clip is chosen: The person speaking agreed to have their voice cloned. It is not repeated on the picker, on the bench, or on the take.

Binding. The formats are what the engine can speak from, and nothing wider. wav and mp3. This screen drew m4a as well — the iOS voice-memo default, and the obvious thing to accept — and it was wrong: capture succeeded and every dispatch against that voice then failed at the engine, which is exactly the mid-take failure §1.3 exists to prevent. A memo recorded on a phone is still a filed artifact and 69a still lists it; it is not a clip this can clone from. Transcoding is the way to widen this, and pretending is not.

The engine row, the bench read and the path from a kept recording back to a sheet are 74e–74g. Measured on an RTX 3080: 39s to load plus 41s to compile before the first line, which does not amortise across launches, and a steady RTF 1.1 — a line takes about as long as it plays. Peak 5.4 GB VRAM against a stated 6 GB floor.

Binding. Music is a fourth bench mode, not a screen of its own: the mode pills, the take strip, the price line and Keep · file as artifact are the ones every other mode already uses. The composer asks for two things and no more — a STYLE line and LYRICS — because the route requires both and neither can be derived from the other. Lyrics are always the author's to accept: the helper drafts into its own dialog and nothing reaches the song until Use these words is pressed, so a generation never carries words nobody read. The helper names who wrote the draft and its length, the way every other model-backed control states its model. There is no length control at all, and that is a decision rather than an omission: minimax-music-3 declares its duration an upper bound — the model stops earlier and reports what it actually made — so a chip would not buy a song of that length, only a ceiling. For a song with lyrics the length is implied by the words. The request goes at the route's own default and the price line says up to rather than ~, because the truth is at most, not about. If a thirty-second sting or a three-minute bed is ever wanted, a length control has to come back somewhere. A take states the model, the length and the price, and its waveform shows played against unplayed exactly as a voice take does.

The row and the route already ship (minimax-music-3, priced per second, capability music); this turn is the surface that reaches them, and would be the first thing in the app ever to enqueue capability: "music". Filing lands the track in the world's Artifacts like any other bench take — the production spine is deliberately out of scope here.

Binding. The engine row states its source — YOUR INSTALL, YOUR URL · NEVER SPAWNED, NOT INSTALLED, Arke-managed — and detection order is user direction, then a found install, then the managed download, which is offered last and labelled fetched only if nothing above is chosen. A disabled recipe carries one clause with both figures where figures exist (Needs 12 GB VRAM. This machine has 10 GB.) and the cloud alternative where one does; an unmeasurable floor reads VRAM could not be measured. The ‹n› GB floor was not checked. and the recipe still dispatches. A URL-only engine's recipes are disabled with exactly Arke cannot verify this engine's files — never wording that implies the files are missing. An engine below the supported floor reads incompatible, never unreachable: it answered, so the reason names the version (ComfyUI 0.2.7 is older than the 0.3.45 floor Arke supports.) and a recipe broken by a missing node names that node, so one recipe can fail where the others still run. The pre-flight refusal names FILE / PINNED / FOUND / SENT with truncated digests and SENT nothing. A held local job's resubmit is priced as GPU time, no charge, never as money; a job orphaned by a changed engine location fails with the engine this job ran on is no longer configured and is never resumed against the new engine. Weight rows are per file: each shows its size, Skip is per file, and a file already in the user's folder reads found in your folder — no download control is drawn for it.

Implements SPEC-021 §2.2, §2.4, §2.7, §2.11–§2.12 and issue 354's design turn. The engine section lives inside the Settings dialog drawn in 22a, replacing its sketched local-video rows; the picker rows extend the model picker's standing capability-copy conventions. Engine states are drawn once each: user path 72a, absent-with-offers 72b, managed and running 72c, user URL 72d, incompatible 72h. Mirrored to the Prototype: 72a as the Settings · local engines pane — the one state the clickable prototype needs to make the section navigable.

Binding. World Chat opens on a new conversation, not on a list. /w/:worldId/chat is a conversation nobody has said anything in yet — the eyebrow-and-h1 head reading New conversation, an empty transcript, and a composer ready for the first sentence. The list screen it replaces is gone: a screen whose only job is choosing which conversation to read stands in front of the thing the feature exists for, and every visit paid for it. Reading an existing one keeps its own address, /chat/:conversationId, and both draw the same screen — the rail, the transcript and the 470px panel do not rearrange between them.

Binding. Nothing is created until something is said. Landing on /chat writes no record; the conversation is created by the first message and titled from it, as it already is. A rail full of empty New conversation rows is then impossible by construction rather than by tidying. The create and the message stay two frames: the message goes once the conversation is open, never in the same tick.

Binding. The history rail is the production rail’s geometry — 236px, a right border, no tint. It is navigation between conversations rather than the content of one, and the app already draws navigation that way; the 470px rail on --muted stays the one tinted column because it is the only one holding something to decide. What is left for the conversation is 654px at the 1360px frame, which is the width Story’s conversation column already has (44a) — a bubble is capped at 440px, so the column gives up nothing.

Binding. A row is its title, and grows a second line only when the conversation is owed something. 2 waiting on you in --warning under the title, and nothing under a row that is merely open: status is not worth a permanent second line in a rail that is scanned rather than read. Nothing may live in the rail that can only be reached by expanding it again — starting a conversation is the whole point of the screen and must not cost two clicks. The conversation column reads 842px collapsed.

Renaming is not offered, because nothing behind the screen can do it.

Binding. The third mode is Voice, not Audio. The mode row has carried an Audio pill since 68b without a screen behind it. Every speech model the studio ships is text-to-speech; a mode called Audio promises music and sound design that no route here can make, and a mode that promises what it cannot do is the same failure as a control the model cannot honour. The pill is renamed in both documents.

Binding. A voice that reads is not a voice that belongs to someone. Choosing a voice on the bench never assigns it to a character. A character’s voice is recorded on their sheet, is versioned, and is cited; a reading voice belongs to one recording and to nothing else. The picker states which voices a character already uses as data on the row — Bray Half-Hitch beside Corr — and picking that row still only reads. The action is labelled Read with this voice for that reason, and assignment stays where the character is.

Binding. The words are the content, not a description of it. In voice mode the composer body holds what will be said, verbatim — not a prompt describing a performance. It follows that the enhancer does not appear here: rewriting somebody’s line is editing the script, not enhancing a prompt.

Binding. A per-character price is exact, and carries no tilde. Speech is billed per character and the characters are already typed, so the figure beside Generate is the price rather than a ceiling. Binding. No references, no keyframes, and no lane offering them. A text-to-speech route takes neither, so both lanes leave the composer in voice mode rather than standing there to refuse a pick. Binding. A screen labels; it does not explain. The reasoning for a design lives in this document, and the rules on it are addressed to the people building the thing — not to the person using it. A surface carries names, counts, states and refusals, and nothing whose job is to teach: no sentence describing what the button about to be pressed will do, no note explaining why a control is arranged as it is, no reassurance that the work is safe. A refusal is the one explanation a screen owes, and it is one clause, on the thing refused — this model takes no audio, not a paragraph above the grid. Where a label and a sentence say the same thing, the sentence goes: Keep · file as artifact already says nothing is filed until you keep it. Turn 68’s screens are cut back in place under this rule, and it holds for every screen drawn after it.

Binding. One picker, wherever a reference is asked for. The bench’s + References, its empty reference tile, and the reference slot of the standard dialog (65a) all open the same surface with the same three sources — World artifacts · This session · Upload — in that order, because the answer is nearly always something the world already holds. Where it opens decides its frame, not its content: on a full-screen surface it is a dialog; asked for from inside a dialog it takes that dialog’s own frame and returns with a back arrow, because a layer on a layer is the thing 41c forbade. The brief behind it is never disturbed — picking is not submitting, and cancelling returns to exactly the words that were there.

Binding. Everything that travels is an artifact first. There is no third category of “attached file”: an upload files into the world as it arrives — named, dated, and visible in Artifacts — and is only then picked, which is what makes it citable in the next brief and auditable in the next ledger. This is true even if the generation is never run, and it is true of a take made on the bench: the session lane offers the session’s own takes, and picking an unkept one keeps it rather than sending an object that exists nowhere.

Binding. The token is shown at the pick, not after it. A file being picked displays the name it will carry — Image 4, Audio 2 — and a file already riding shows the name it already has, so the same artifact is never added twice under two names. The footer names every token being added in one line, because the whole reason for the pick is usually to write that token into the brief. Numbers come from the session’s next free slot and are never reused within it, per 68b.

Binding. What cannot travel is shown with its reason, never hidden. A control the model cannot honour leaves the composer (68b); a file the model cannot accept stays and says why — this model takes no audio, a document cannot be sent — because the file genuinely exists and quietly filtering it reads as the world having lost it. The capacity is stated before the pick, in the unit the model is actually bounded in — images count, audio and video are aggregate seconds: 3 of 4 images · 0:12 of 1:00 audio. Sound and motion are budgeted by length rather than by file wherever the manifest bounds them that way, so a single recording longer than what is left is refused at the tile with its length on it, and a count nobody could source is never shown. All of it is drawn from the same model manifest the composer and the request builder read. At the ceiling the picker asks which one is replaced; it never accepts a fifth and drops one on the way out, which is the silent-truncation failure 65a was written against. A result set says where it ends and what it searched — including how many of its own results cannot be sent — and a search that finds nothing offers the same upload lane rather than an empty rectangle.

Binding. The bench is reached from Artifacts and files back into Artifacts. Generate stands beside New artifact on the world’s Artifacts page, and is the only door to it — a production never grows one, because a production already has a Generate of its own with shots to answer to. Nothing made here belongs to a production: a kept take files as a world artifact with the provenance every take carries (brief, references, model, seed, cost), shows as made here, and is linkable to canon, characters and shots afterwards like any other file. Spend is real spend — it ledgers to the world and appears in Activity exactly as a production’s does, because the money left the same account.

Binding. The dialog is for a slot; the bench is for no slot. 65a stands unchanged wherever a picture has somewhere to land — the master look, key art, a main photo, a location view — and those surfaces may not open the bench, because a bench take answers no question and would leave the slot still empty. The bench exists for the opposite case and is the only surface allowed to ask for a picture with nowhere for it to go. Where the dialog draws Accept, the bench draws Keep, and the two are the same act on different objects.

Binding. A reference is an artifact, and the prompt names it. Every tile on the bench is a file the world already holds (or one dropped in, which files on arrival), and each carries a token — Image 1, Image 2, Audio 1 — that the brief may cite inline. The tile and the chip are one object: removing the tile strikes its chip and renumbers nothing, because a token that shifts would silently rewrite every brief that used it. Tokens are per-session and stable for its life. A reference the chosen model cannot accept is refused at the tile with the reason, not dropped quietly at dispatch.

Binding. The mode picks the controls; the model picks what the controls may say. Image · Video · Audio is one choice, and it decides which row of settings exists — duration and sound belong to video and are absent, not disabled, under image. Within a mode the model narrows further, and a control it cannot honour leaves rather than greying: a model that takes no keyframes shows no Keyframe tab, and the composer says so in a line rather than a tooltip. The character counter’s ceiling is the model’s, read from limits.maxPromptChars — 3500 here is not a house number — it is shown before the brief is over it, and over it Generate refuses rather than truncating: a brief cut at the end loses the shot list, not the adjectives. A model that publishes no cap gets no counter, by the same rule that takes the Keyframe tab away — a counter is a promise about a refusal, and one measured against a number nobody could source would refuse briefs the model would have taken. The estimate on the button follows every control above it, per 65a.

Binding. The strip is the session, not a gallery. Takes are numbered in the order they were asked for, oldest at the top, and the number is the take’s name everywhere else on the screen; a queued take holds its number before it has an image, so nothing renumbers when one fails. Selecting a take restores the brief that made it into the composer, which is what makes re-running an edit rather than a retype. Leaving the bench does not end the session — it is titled, listed, and reopened with its strip and its references intact — and View latest exists because scrolling back through it is normal, not an error state.

Binding. Every generation dialog offers a picture to look at. 62a named three things the dialog asks for and the second was a picture to look at; five of the six surfaces were asking two, because only the master look had anywhere to keep one. That absence was a thing to build, not a reason to drop the row — so staging is keyed by surface under one directory, one image per key, on disk so it survives a reload and so the bytes never cross into the renderer. The key is a fixed vocabulary plus a slug, validated at the door, because it becomes a folder name and a free-text one would be a traversal wearing the name of a feature.

Binding. What a surface must carry outranks what an author attached. A character’s identity anchor and a location’s establishing view go first; the staged image rides in whatever room the model has left, and carries its own role — style, not identity, because a provider that reads roles must not be told this face is the one to preserve. It is dropped when the ask it was staged for is accepted, and kept when the result is rejected: the usual answer to a rejection is to run it again, and running it again with the picture you had just chosen is the point of having staged it. The estimate counts it, like every other image.

Binding. Both of the world’s pictures clear the fold. Key art sat two thirds down the other column, so the page about the world’s pictures showed one and made you scroll for the other. They stack: the master look takes the height that is left, key art a fixed 168px band beneath it, and on a short window the look gives way rather than the band. The pictures take the width the window has — a fixed 680 stranded the surplus in the other column as an empty spacer, 320px of it on a 1400 window — while the reading column keeps a measure, because prose does not improve past about sixty characters.

Binding. Pressing Generate says so on the press, not on the first job event. Between the click and anything observable there is a round trip — send, resolve a model, price it, enqueue — and the button sat unchanged through all of it, which is how somebody who has just bought four images comes to buy eight. The label reads Generating… from the click and through both windows: the one before a job exists, and the run once the host can see it. It is cleared by a timeout as well as by the answer, because a request refused without ever becoming a job would otherwise leave the button saying it forever.

Binding. The dialog asks for four things, not three, and the fourth is how many. 62a’s order stands and the count joins the row that already carries the model — 1 to 4, one number named once and shared by the frame that validates it, the control that offers it and the request builder that fans it out. Four previews are four jobs, each separately priced, ledgered and cancellable, and each landing under its own name: four jobs sharing one landing name is four charges and one file, which is exactly what "generate looks does not work" was.

Binding. A control that multiplies the bill must show the bill. The estimate moved off the full variant’s button group and onto the controls themselves, because the standard dialog draws its own actions and had therefore never priced anything — survivable while a dialog meant one image, and not survivable the moment the count arrived. The figure is for the whole set and moves with every control above it.

Binding. What came back sits beside what was asked for, and is chosen there. The right column holds the set as a 2×2 whatever its size — a grid that reflowed to one big tile for a single result would change the size of the thing being judged according to how many there were of it — and it carries three states that are genuinely different: nothing asked for, something in flight, and something to choose between. In flight is never "ready when you are": the money is already spent, and that sentence to somebody who has just pressed Generate is the complaint this column was built from. Submitting does not close the dialog, because the previews land in it. One offer is answered in one place — the page behind says only that something is waiting, and reopens the dialog to deal with it.

Binding. Every surface that asks for a picture asks for it in this dialog. Its one escape hatch is what travels — which references ride along, and what the chosen model will drop — because that genuinely differs per surface. The two-phase wizard goes with it: the character sheet used to hide its settings the moment you pressed Generate, so a result you did not like left you looking at a screen with no words on it. Two columns mean the brief never leaves, and a failed dispatch is a reason on the composer rather than a fourth screen with a button back to the one you were on. A look inherited from the world is shown in the box, not behind an Override toggle — the words being sent were never on screen, and overriding meant writing a replacement for something you could not read. The words, the model, the size and the count never move, and a surface that wants its own arrangement of those has rebuilt the problem the dialog was written to end. A surface with nothing to show keeps the single column: undefined previews is "this offer is answered elsewhere", which is not the same as an empty set. Where saying no is a decision it gets a button, not a link — rejecting a take, discarding a set — beside the primary, because somebody who does not want what came back must answer as deliberately as somebody who does. A surface producing exactly one composite pre-selects it: a click on a lone tile before you may answer it exists only because the column can hold four.

It belongs here: this is the page about the world’s pictures, and a page about the world’s pictures carries both of them or it is not that page. The key-art frame follows 62a’s rule exactly — the two doors live on the picture, revealed on :hover and :focus-within, always in the document.

Binding. Neither picture ever stands in for the other. The master-look frame no longer falls back to key art when no look is set: it showed the key art under Generate and Upload buttons that made a master look, so the one gesture the picture invited was the one gesture it did not perform. An unset picture says it is unset — two empty frames on a young world, which is the truth and is also the only state from which both doors mean what they say. Each caption names which of the two it is, and the key-art caption states the distinction that governs everything else: a master look is a treatment sent to models, key art is a picture of the world that is never sent anywhere — which is precisely why key art may carry the faces a master look may not.

Binding. Key art is asked for in the same dialog as everything else (62a), and its prompt box opens as the words the app would otherwise have sent — the look’s description, the logline, the tone, the genre, composed by the one function both ends share, so what the author edits is exactly what would have gone. An edited prompt is sent as written and silences the art director: the studio writes the prompt only while nobody else has, because a rewrite on top of an author’s own words is the studio’s taste in front of theirs. The standing constraint suffix is appended either way and is not the author’s to drop. An unedited box sends no prompt at all rather than sending its contents back — the two look identical from the screen and mean opposite things at the other end.

Binding. A generation dialog draws no reference row where the surface has nowhere to stage one. Key art has no reference slot in this turn: there is no staged-reference path for it in the world, and a slot that opened a picker whose result had no home is worse than no slot. The row is therefore absent, not disabled, and the estimate beneath prices no reference image — undefined is a third state and is not null, which still means "attach one".
