Binding. The world overview holds no controls over the world’s pictures. The hero is a name, a logline and a cast — a way in, not a workbench — so the key-art row (Generate key art from the logline, Upload an image, a model picker and the keep-or-discard offer) leaves it, and with it the clause in 61a that put key art here because "the image it feeds is the thing on screen". It is not: the thing on screen is the world. Removing the row leaves the world’s key art with no setter at all, which is a hole to close deliberately rather than by leaving four buttons under a title — see Try next.

Binding. Everything below the fold is derived and clickable, and every figure states what is outstanding beneath it. The glance is four figures over one hairline-divided box — counts of the world’s own entities, never a production’s guests — and each carries a second line naming what is unsettled about that count (N proposed changes, N waiting for approval, N still a sketch), falling back to a settled statement rather than to nothing — the line is pinned at 15px and clipped, so four cells hold one height whatever the world has in it. The figures are figures, not buttons: the tab row above is how those screens are reached, and a second set of doors to the same seven places would be the inventory this page has twice been cleared of.

Binding. Bands on the production tile are pinned — frame 128, format 13, title 19, foot 15 — and the title and foot are clipped to one line each, so three productions with a one-word title, a logline and no shots at all still sit level. A percentage is shown only where shots exist to divide; a story production carries its scene and chapter counts and no bar, because a completion figure over nothing countable is invented. The row takes as many columns as there are productions, to a maximum of three and a minimum of two — two productions are two halves, never two thirds and a hole, and one is never a card the width of the page with a 128px frame in it.

Binding. What needs a person is one line at the foot of the page, or it is absent. It names at most two things — a staged proposal, an open canon thread — each as subject · what kind of decision with the verb that settles it, and it never renders at zero. Only the subject clips: the kind and the verb are flex:none, because a proposal’s summary is a whole sentence and leaving the kind after it in one clipped run made the one thing this line exists to say the first thing the ellipsis ate. This is the narrow re-entry of what turn 44 pulled off this page: the panels that stacked here were screens' worth of content pushing the world’s own entrances below the fold, whereas one line beneath the productions costs nothing above it. The chrome’s warning dot remains the guarantee of findability — this line is a convenience, so it may be capped at two and may sit off-screen without anything being lost.

Binding. The art-direction page carries the look, the offer to change it, and what the look used to be — and nothing else. The reach counts (what follows this look) belong beside Accept on the propose screen, where they are about to matter; the overrides (not following it) belong to the work that carries them; and the world’s key art is set on the world hub, where the image it feeds is the thing on screen. Three inventories on one page had pushed the look itself into a third of a column.

Binding. The two doors onto a picture live on the picture. Generate and Upload appear over the master look on hover, because the thing being replaced is that image and a control a column away does not say so. They are always in the document and only ever faded — revealed on :hover and :focus-within, so the keyboard reaches them; mounting them on pointer entry would put them out of reach entirely. An empty look washes with its own surface rather than a dark scrim, which over a light card is a smear.

Binding. Every generation is asked for in one dialog, and it asks for three things in one order: the words, a picture to look at, then who makes it. The prompt opens as the subject’s own words — the look’s description here — and is sent as written, with no art-director rewrite and with the surface’s standing safety clause appended after it, which is not the author’s to drop. An empty prompt cannot be submitted. The reference image is optional, one at a time, and staged in the world rather than held in the renderer, so it survives a reload and the bytes never cross into the client; it is dropped once the offer it helped make is settled, so it can never join a later generation nobody attached it to. It rides along only where the chosen model declares reference slots, and where it rides it is priced. The model, the size and the shape are all chosen in the dialog, by the same resolver the button’s enabled state asks, so the two cannot disagree about what will be sent.

Binding. A model row is offered the shapes it declares, plus the one it would have used anyway — from limits.aspects where it enumerates them, from the standard set narrowed to aspectRange where it gives a range, and no control at all where it declares neither, because an unverified row runs at the provider’s default and a picker over it would promise what nobody checked. The shape a surface would have produced without a picker comes first, and is the default: opening the dialog and changing nothing must generate exactly what pressing Generate generated before the dialog had controls. A declared list is an offer, not a limit — it is curated, and a row happily takes ratios it was never listed with — so a derived default outside it is folded in rather than corrected away. Snapping it into the list instead would crop every character photograph to a square, and a square identity anchor is a worse mistake than an unlisted ratio. A shape the row would not take is dropped rather than sent, at the request as well as in the picker. Changing the model drops a size or a shape the new row cannot reach, on screen and on the wire together: the segment falling back while the request kept the old value is the same bug in two places. Choosing a shape must not also change the size — a shape is reshaped around the long edge the tier established, and the tier alone decides how big. The reported aspect must describe the pixels beside it on every path, because that string is what a client submitting aspect_ratio would send. The estimate follows all three, computed from the dimensions the request will actually carry rather than an assumed megapixel, and from the surface’s stated orientation rather than one inferred from a workflow it borrowed for its price band.

Binding. A control that opens a list must look like one. The model pill carries a chevron and how many models there are whenever there is more than one, and neither when there is only one, because an affordance that opens a list of one is a small lie. Its accessible name says the count too. This is the rule a badge-shaped pill broke for a year: it had always opened a listbox, and every reader took the routed default for a fixed property of the screen.

Binding. A world carries two pictures and they are never the same field. The master look is part of the look record: one per version, carried into other work for its treatment, and it is what the art-direction hero shows. The key art is a picture of the world and is what the worlds list, the hub hero and the settings backdrop show; it is never sent to a model. Both can be generated or uploaded, and both land as a candidate that is answered rather than applied. A master look is generated from the look’s own description, sent unedited — no art-director rewrite, unlike key art — with a standing clause forbidding people, faces, text and montage, because this is the one asset that rides along with somebody else’s portrait. Accepting a master look is a look change: the image lands under the next version’s name and the record naming it is that next version, so no accepted version is ever given an image that did not exist while it was current; the version it replaces keeps its own image in history. Accepting key art replaces the world’s one key art and does not touch the look or its version. An accepted image keeps the format its bytes carry — world-art.png, world-art.jpg — so the path is read from the world and carried on the picker’s registry row; nothing may assume the extension. One candidate at a time per image: offering again replaces the offer rather than accumulating one per format.

Binding. The heading over a look is typography, never meaning. It is the description’s own opening promoted to display type, and the whole description is what every generation receives — which the screen states in words rather than leaving to be inferred from a bold line above a grey one. A first sentence longer than 120 characters is broken at its own first structural mark (:, ;, an em dash, else the last comma that fits) rather than set entire in 42px. The split never loses a word: heading plus body reads back as the description, and a one-sentence look has no body rather than printing itself twice.

Binding. Every column that ends in a decision scrolls. Both columns of the propose screen end in the control the screen exists for — Set the look on the left, Accept on the right — and the art-direction page ends in its own history, so a short window must crop nothing that can be pressed. A character’s main photo opens the identity reference set it anchors, not a larger copy of itself: the picture is already on screen, and what the anchor is for is the set. Enlarging is unchanged everywhere the picture is the point.

Binding. A staleness report names the files that differed, and a difference must survive a second look before it is reported at all. The app’s own commit refreshes the store’s view only after its bytes land, so a check falling in that window read our own write as another program’s — a world folder that changed outside Arke Studio is a claim that has to be checkable, and a warning that cannot say what changed is a warning nobody can act on.

Binding. The sole spine authority is productions/<id>/spine.json, holding the track artifact id, markers and anchors; nothing is duplicated into production.json, cut.json, scene files or selections. Every edit commits against the file’s base hash, increments revision once, and is change-logged — a stale write is refused and the client reloads, because anchors are never silently merged. The band is 56px of waveform with section markers as full-height rules labelled beneath, and lyric markers as a second label row; the playhead is a 2px rule. Anchors are half-open [startSec, endSec) against the measured track, must satisfy 0 ≤ startSec < endSec ≤ duration, and may not overlap — touching boundaries are valid and an overlap is refused at the drag, not at export. Anchor order governs the cut, not scene order. endSec - startSec is the duration budget wherever spine-aware planning runs; shot.durationSec stays the fallback for unanchored shots and spineless productions, and anchoring never rewrites it. Every anchor is editable both by drag and by typed seconds, which are one edit — a timeline that cannot be typed into cannot be made precise. Nothing is ever stretched, frozen or looped: long material is trimmed from trimInSec, short material plays and then holds a labelled slate, and unanchored shots stay in the tray and are never appended after the song. An orphaned anchor is reported, never auto-removed, and blocks clean export until a person resolves it. Review export is always available with gaps as labelled black; master and social-excerpt are blocked by any orphan, overlap, missing take, unknown duration or shortfall — deterministic trimming alone never blocks. The master track is the bed at 0 dB and never ducks; a shot’s own audio is mute by default or keep-diegetic mixed beneath at a stated gainDb (default −12). Assignment requires measured positive duration and audio presence; a failed probe refuses assignment, never loses the artifact or take, and is retryable locally at no cost. Marker import is previewed and atomic: JSON replaces sections and lyrics, LRC replaces lyrics only, both leave anchors untouched, a single bad row refuses the whole file naming its one-based line, and markers past the measured duration are refused. A production with no spine.json keeps the scene-order cut unchanged, with no migration.

Binding. Art direction carries an audio policy and a list of standing failure modes, on the current record and on every history entry. Music is environmental-only (default) or allow-model-score; subtitles are never and v1 offers no alternative, because Arke’s cut owns titles and burned-in text cannot be moved, translated or removed. Failure modes are at most 20, each at most 300 characters. Defaults are read compatibility, not migration: an older record or history entry resolves to environmental-only, never and [] in memory, and merely opening that world neither rewrites its file nor bumps its version. Changing a policy travels the existing art-direction gate — a staged proposal, a version bump, history preserved, and the ripple named before acceptance; accepted takes keep the policy they were made under. A production may strengthen and never relax. Where the world allows score, the production offers Inherit or Strengthen to environmental-only; where the world already says environmental only, the production shows the inherited state and no control at all — a disabled option invites a question whose answer is that it is never allowed. Production failure modes are additive to the world’s, never a replacement. Merge order at dispatch is world, then production, and both are composed after the shot body: an overridden prompt replaces the body alone, so it can remove neither the constraints nor the final negatives. The merged result is shown in full on the production surface, because a rule nobody can read is a rule nobody can check.

Binding. A production keeps its own cast. A character, place or faction may be owned by one production rather than by the world — a guest — and the guest is a full sheet: it versions, passes the gate, is cited, is retired, takes a reference kit and takes a voice exactly as a world sheet does. Ownership decides where it is shown and nothing else. Cast joins the production rail on both formats, between Dashboard and Story, amending the format-specific rail of 54a: a story has a cast as much as a video does. Its count is the guests — the number the rail can say something true about — because the world’s cast is shared and is counted on the world’s own Cast tab (54c). The screen is two bands, never one list: GUESTS · ONLY IN <title> above, FROM <world> · SHARED below, each with its own count, and the foot of every card says which it is — guest · v1 or character · v5. Both sets are equally castable and a shot cannot tell them apart, so the surface must. The world’s own surfaces exclude guests entirely: the hub’s cast fan, the entity counts and all three ledgers show what the world owns, and a production holding nine guests leaves the world’s character count unchanged. A guest is promoted, never demoted. Promotion clears the owner and moves nothing — the slug, the file, every citation, every take’s provenance and the reference kit all stay — and it cuts a version, so the history shows where it joined the world. There is no way back: a sheet promoted by mistake is retired, the mechanism the product already has for that. A mention never checks scope. @the-barman resolves whoever owns it, the same rule a retired sheet follows, and citing another production’s guest is named at dispatch and not blocked — The barman belongs to the-ledger-of-nights, not to this production — beside the sketch and retired warnings.

Ownership is settled; continuity is not. A one-off that wants the world’s art direction, voices and tone but not its canon — an ad, a music video, a what-if — is a different question from whose the barman is, and the next turn asks it.

Binding. A location has a reference kit, and its detail screen carries two tabs — Overview and Reference. The first accepted view is named Establishing view; it is what a location card and the detail hero show, and every later view is generated anchored to it. At most six views are active at once, and the seventh is refused before generation rather than after payment. Panel order is the establishing view first, then acceptance order — never alphabetical, never the order they were generated in. Panels are labelled PANEL 01 - ESTABLISHING VIEW, PANEL 02 - REVERSE ANGLE, and so on, and the prompt's binding preamble states that same map, so the spatial-layout block's spatial block can cite a fixture by the panel it appears in. The location sheet is assembled locally and never generated: it costs nothing, it is rebuilt on every acceptance, and identical views in an identical order must produce an identical file. Accepting a duplicate name asks first and, on confirmation, supersedes the old record while leaving panel order unchanged; a superseded view keeps its history and its immutable take. A failed assembly changes nothing — the candidate stays unreviewed, the previous sheet stays the one shots carry, and retrying spends nothing.

Characters and locations now both answer “what does this look like from more than one side”. What neither answers yet is when: the day pass and the night pass of one room are two views here, and a prop that leaves a fridge is nothing at all. That is the state question, and it is the prop-state exploration's to settle.

Binding. A decision belongs where the point is, amending 41a, which had the conversation decide nothing and deciding happen exactly twice. It cost what it saved: a conversation produces a dozen points of which two are wrong, and saying so meant carrying all twelve to another screen to reject two there. Every point carries Save and Reject — ghost, sm, on their own line beneath the sentence, because a point is often two lines and controls beside it squeeze the words into a column narrower than they need. Save writes. It stages and accepts in one motion, the same rule the art-direction form follows for a look somebody typed, so history, ripples and the change log are those of a reviewed proposal — the review is the press. The rail’s action is Accept all, still at its foot, full width, size="lg", with the caption beneath: it writes what is left and closes the conversation. Talking still changes nothing, and the composer still says so. Two things a press may not decide. A proposal carrying an open choice — is this a new rule, or a change to that one — waits on the approvals screen, which is now the exception rather than the road every change travels. And an atomic group is one change: saving one member writes them all as a single proposal, rejecting one rejects them all, and a group whose members rewrite the same file, or which mixes a look change with other changes, is refused by name rather than half written. Every decision carries the revision the rail was showing, its group’s members included, so a point corrected by talking since is refused rather than written as it was. The rest of 41a stands: the split, the 470px rail, the composer, the shell, and the one-column fall below 1100px.

What the approvals screen is for, now that most changes never reach it: it holds questions a press could not answer and proposals an accept could not land, which are two different things wearing one label. The next turn gives them different words.

Binding. A take is decided where it was made. The Generate workspace is the one surface a production take is accepted or rejected from. Stills leaves the rail and becomes the workspace's second lens — the seg reads Shot · Scene · Contact sheet — showing the same frame/still takes as a set, decided one at a time, exactly as the retired screen did. Binding. The rail is the format's. A production's rail offers only the surfaces its format can use: story shows Dashboard · Story · Chapters · Audio · Exports; video keeps the rail it has. Nothing is disabled or greyed — a surface that does not apply is not present, and no story screen mentions shots, takes, clips or dispatch. The switch card counts what the format counts: seconds of cut for video, chapters for story (novel · 24 chapters, never story · 0s cut). The dashboard resumes the format's unit of work — for story, the chapter furthest from done, with Story as the way in; the day-one seed framing stays a video affair. Audio and Exports are the format's too: for story, Audio is the world's audio artifacts alone — no dialogue rows, no voice-line dispatch — and Exports offers no cut render: the manuscript exporter is designed, not yet built, the pane says so, and the world-folder export keeps living there so the chapters travel whole. A chapter's word count follows its prose: a direct save recounts words in the frontmatter, so the chapter tree and the dashboard never report a stale count.
A destination appears once per screen. The character sheet's Reference, More looks and Voice live in its tab row; the buttons that repeated the first two under the essence are gone from 3a, and the action row keeps only what the tabs do not offer: Edit the sheet and its companions. Two controls to one place is a choice; one place per control is the rule.
Settings asks one question about models. “Which model does this work” was answered on two tabs in two vocabularies — capabilities on Who does what, writing agents on Agents. 54b keeps the one tab and folds the agents beneath an Advanced disclosure on it, closed by default: the routing defaults are the everyday answer, the per-agent overrides are the expert's, and a user who never opens Advanced loses nothing — every agent already defaults to whatever the harness is set to. The disclosure is a control, not a tab: it does not survive navigation and never becomes a destination.
The world keeps one Cast tab. Characters, locations and factions are one kind of thing — a sheet — and a new world showed three empty tabs to prove it. 54c puts one Cast pill in the world navigation, lit on all three ledgers, with a chip row — Characters · 6 / Locations · 4 / Factions · 3 — moving between them. Each ledger keeps its address and its presentation: the cast ledger, the location grid and the faction cards are unchanged behind the chips, deep links keep working, and the counts ride on the chips so an empty kind says so before you visit it. The world navigation drops from nine pills to seven.
A legend earns its line. Nearly every screen ended with a sentence explaining the data model — the app teaching its own architecture on every page, permanently, to a user who learned it on page three. The rule from turn 53 — the controls say it — now applies to the line under them: a legend may warn (the cut is a projection; an unfinished film exports black slates; a running session keeps the settings it started with) but it may not restate what the screen already shows. Gone: the audio screen reciting that voices come from the sheets when every row names its sheet, the generate workspace explaining that an override is an override, the looks screen saying its own lede a second time, the appearance and runtime panes' architecture footnotes, and the sheet detail's index asides. What warns, stays; what re-teaches, goes.

All five came from one walk through the app taken as a user rather than as its author. The next walk should start where this one stopped: the take reviewed in four places, and the two workspaces still competing to spend a scene (53e is the settled surface; the Generate workspace has not yet conceded).

Binding. Build the plain version first, and add to it only once the plain version has been used. Every rule below is that one applied.
A default must look like a control. On 53a the profile's defaults are dropdowns with their own labels, not printed values with a chevron glued on, because a value the user cannot tell is editable is a value they will not edit. Each of the three kinds carries a banner, so the choice is made by looking rather than by reading. What was cut is the point of the screen: no summary grid, no idea field, no paragraph explaining that a profile only sets defaults — the controls say it. Step two asks two things: which kind, and the handful of numbers that differ between them.
An empty production is a place to start writing, not a briefing. 53b drops the day-one framing, the world inventory and both seed rails. The world is not announced because the production is already inside it — the rail says so and nothing else needs to. What is left is a heading, a composer and two ways in. Seeds return only when the plain path has been used and found wanting; a suggestion engine on an empty page is a guess about a workflow nobody has run yet.
Beats are gone. An episode is its promise and its scenes, and a scene's own one-line description is the brief. The indirection beats added — a named unit of change that scenes were cited against — bought a many-to-many map that a five-scene episode does not need, and it cost a whole screen (46b) to explain. 53c is one episode screen where there were two: the conversation on the left, the promise and the scenes in order on the right. A script belongs to a scene and to nothing above it.
The board is where a shot is changed. Selecting a panel opens it in place: the prompt is an editable field, not a printed one, and the model, size, length and references are the same dropdowns as everywhere else. An edited prompt says it was edited and offers the assembled one back, because the assembled version is regenerated from a world that keeps moving and a hand-written one is not. The board carries the whole-scene total as well as the per-shot one, so there is no separate screen to visit before spending.
The board is the only surface a scene is spent from. Turn 52’s separate plan is retired: it showed the same four shots, the same coverage and the same prices as the board, one screen earlier, and a second place to read the same thing is a second place to keep correct. What the plan was right about moves onto the board and stays: the warning bar in the words of the specific thing that is wrong, the blocks no shot covers with one action to fix them, and the whole-scene estimate against seconds owned and seconds asked. At rest the board is the surface — four across, scene order, every panel priced. With one shot open it is the split, which is the same rule every other pair in this workspace follows: comparison earns the surface, authoring one object keeps the split.

Try next: “the board once takes exist, and whether editing a prompt still belongs there” · “an episode of twenty scenes, and where the flat list stops working” · “step two for a format with only one kind” · “the empty production for someone on their fourth, not their first”

Binding. The plan is one screen between accepting a scene and spending on it, and it replaces the warning list in 14b. It is a surface — shots run left to right in scene order, which is cut order, and the row is never sorted by anything else. Each shot shows the script it covers, without being clicked: the point of the screen is scanning whether the coverage is right, and a plan you have to open four times cannot be scanned. Blocks with no shot appear as a dashed row beneath, quoting the lines that will be missing, with one action to add a shot. Nothing here spends. The only control that spends says what it will cost in its own label — Generate 4 shots · $5.46 — and there is a per-shot equivalent, so a single retry never re-runs the scene. The estimate is the whole scene, not one request, and it is the number the product has been missing: per-shot cost, scene total, seconds asked against seconds owned. Where a route rounds a length up, the shot says both (3s planned · 4s asked), because the difference is paid for. Opening a shot shows the prompt as its parts, never as a blob, and every part names its source: art direction, the scene, the location sheet, the shot, the mentioned sheets at their versions, the script block the line came from. Nobody typed it, so the screen says what wrote it. Beside it, what travels: each reference marked CARRIED or DROPPED with its mode and the reason it did not fit, because a dropped face is the most common cause of a take that looks wrong and it is knowable before the money moves. Writing your own prompt is offered as replacing the assembled one for that shot only, and the offer states its own consequence — the sheet will move past it later and you will be told. Warnings sit above the plan and never block, in the words of the specific thing that is wrong, which is 43’s discipline applied to spend.

Export sheet

Binding. The board is the visual read of one scene and takes the surface — a grid of four panels across the 1124px content column with a 12px gutter, the same grid the season board uses and the same the compiler already writes. Panels stand in the shape the scene will be watched in: a 9:16 production boards portrait, so the aspect chosen at creation is visible here rather than discovered at dispatch. Order is scene order, always; the board never sorts by anything else, because its whole job is reading the scene the way an audience will. Compiling is local, free and repeatable — the same scene state produces the same image — and it files nothing. Exporting files exactly one artifact, which is why the two are separate controls and why recompiling twenty times leaves the artifacts folder untouched. A gap is a panel, not a missing one. A shot with no accepted frame keeps its place, its number, its duration and what it covers, because a scene half-generated still has to be readable in order. Staleness is per panel. The board records the scene version it compiled from, and turn 49’s block flags say which shots the change touched — so a script edit dims the two panels it affected and leaves the others alone (51b). Recompiling is cheap; knowing where to look is the scarce thing. A panel whose shot now covers nothing is marked and kept, and recompiling will not remove it, because that is a decision and not a stale picture. With no frames at all the board still renders (51c): duration, order, title and coverage are legible without a single image, which makes it a shot list before it is a storyboard. Finally, this board is not the thing sent to a model. It is editorial, it may hold placeholders, and the provider-ready storyboard is compiled per pass from the accepted shots at dispatch. Two artefacts, one shot plan, and neither is a second script.

Binding. A split is not an event. It is an edit of the block being split and an insert of a new one, and the change log holds exactly those two entries. A merge is an edit and a delete. Neither gets its own record, its own warning, or its own rule, because turn 49 already says what an edited block and a new block do to coverage, and a third vocabulary would be a third thing to keep consistent. The split affordance is a convenience in the editor; underneath, nothing new happened. The block being split keeps its id, and the new half is inserted after it with a fresh one — A09, never A02b and never a renumber, so every citation still points where it pointed. A retired id is never reused: if a merge deletes A09, no later block is A09, because an id that comes back means a citation in an old take or a landed job silently resolves to text nobody wrote. The one thing the product cannot infer is asked out loud. When the split block was covered, the shot must land somewhere, and the editor offers which half, or both (50a) with the consequence of the highlighted option stated in words before it is taken. It defaults to the block that kept the id, because that is the least surprising answer and the one that requires no guess about intent — a two-shot at a door could be the hands or the waiting, and only the person who framed it knows. Choosing both is a legitimate answer and an explicit one; what is forbidden is the product choosing it silently, which is the rule turn 49 already binds. Everything downstream is unchanged: the flags are covers text that changed and covers nothing, both already in the vocabulary, and a shot left covering nothing is kept, never deleted (50c), because camera and audio are authored work and a merge is not a reason to discard them.

Binding. Script first, coverage second. A scene is written before anything decides how it is filmed, and the workspace carries the same four-view strip the season does — Script, Coverage, Board, Takes — under turn 46’s test: Script authors one object so it keeps the split and the 470px rail; Coverage is a blocks-against-shots mapping, so it takes the 1124px surface. A script block is a slugline, an action or a line of dialogue, and it carries an id assigned once — S01, A01, D01 — with order as a separate field. Ids are never renumbered: a block inserted between A03 and A04 becomes A08 (49c), because renumbering would silently repoint every shot that cites one, which is the same reasoning that keeps sheet ids stable and chapter order in frontmatter. Shots cite blocks; blocks do not belong to shots. One shot may answer several blocks, and a block may be answered by more than one — a wide and a close on the same line is coverage, not duplication. Only action and dialogue are coverable; a slugline is context and is never counted. Dialogue lives in the block, and the shot cites it rather than restating the line, so there is one authored copy of what is said, for the same reason mentions are the only cast list. An edit flags coverage; it never repairs or breaks it silently. Rewriting a covered block keeps its id, advances the block, and marks every citing shot covers text that changed — out of date, not broken — exactly as an overridden prompt is flagged when its sheet advances. Cutting a covered block leaves the shot in place marked covers nothing: it is kept rather than deleted, because deleting a shot on the user’s behalf destroys camera and audio work to tidy a link. Nothing blocks. Uncovered action and dialogue join the named warnings before dispatch, and the ending of a scene is called out by name, because the last blocks are the ones most often left uncovered and the cheapest to fix before the money moves.

Binding. The Story workspace has four views and one tab strip: Season, Episodes, Arcs, Direction. Every one of them now exists, because a tab that leads nowhere is the same broken promise as an empty state that says nothing. The layout follows what the view is for, which is turn 46’s rule carried to its conclusion: Season and Direction each author one object, so they keep the split and the 470px rail; Episodes and Arcs are comparisons across the season, so they take the 1124px surface with the conversation as a row at the foot. The tab strip sits in the same place in both — the head of whichever column is the draft — so switching views moves the body and never the navigation. A production with no episodes shows three tabs, not four greyed out: a short film has no season to compare, so the Episodes tab does not exist for it and turn 44’s untabbed overview becomes the Season view of the same strip. Inheritance is shown, not hidden. The Season view carries the Series engine as a read-only card saying which seasons it governs and that editing it opens the Series, because a field that silently edits two seasons is the drift the world model exists to prevent. Direction shows the world look first, then what the season narrows, as lines against it — never a replacement image — and states in a dashed block that no other production moves. An arc lane is a thing that changes, not a character, and the grid marks only three cells per lane in words as well as colour: SETUP, TURN, PAYOFF. A lane with no payoff is called out at the top of the view and marked in --destructive in the finale column, because an arc that never lands is the one structural fault a season board cannot show.

Binding. Format is structure, profile is defaults. Format — story, video, stills — decides which surfaces exist, and stays step one. Profile is step two, sets values, and creates no second entity: a micro-drama is a Video production with the same scenes, shots, takes and cut as a short film, and the dialog says so in a line rather than leaving it to be inferred. This is where the numbers turn 45 assumes are actually chosen — the season board’s seven episodes, its 45–75 seconds and its vertical frame all originate on this screen, and until it existed the board was showing a season nobody had specified. Defaults render as chips carrying their value, each openable, never as a checkbox whose effect you have to guess; the four that are not single values sit beneath as named cards. Step two scales to what the profile actually decides (47b): a short film sets two things and says so, and what it does not set is stated in a dashed block rather than shown as empty controls — the same discipline 43c uses for a seed source with nothing in it. Where a format has one profile, step two does not render at all and the step counter reads step 1 of 1; a step that asks a question with one answer is a toll. The action keeps turn 43a’s rule and names where it lands, which for a series means naming both things it makes — Create Series and open day one, opening Season 1, never a Series index.

Binding. The episode workspace is the split again, not a third pattern: conversation left, a 470px rail on --muted, the action at its foot. That settles what turn 45 could have been read to open. One rule covers both — comparison earns the surface, authoring one object keeps the split. A season is compared against itself, so it takes the page; an episode, an overview and a scene are each one object being written, so they keep the rail. Nothing else may claim the surface without that argument. An episode therefore has two views and they are not the same shape. Beats is the workspace, where one episode is written, and it keeps the split (46a). What realises it is a many-to-many mapping of beats against scenes — a comparison by the same test the season passed — so it takes the 1124px surface (46b). The test is not how important a view is or how much it holds; it is whether its value comes from reading rows against each other. The rail holds the promise first — opens, turn, closes, then hook and cliffhanger — because an episode is one audience promise and its beats only make sense underneath it. Beats come second, ordered, each naming what changes rather than what is seen. A beat cites the scenes that realise it and never contains them (46b): one beat may be carried by two scenes, one scene may be cited by two episodes, and a beat with no scene says no scene yet and offers to draft one rather than hiding. This is the folder tree the brief refuses, drawn: the rows are a derived view over links, so the same scene appearing under episode 3 and episode 4 is correct rather than duplicated, and an episode that ends inside a continuous scene is expressible. Scenes claimed by no beat are surfaced at the foot with a count, because a scene nothing points at is the one thing this view exists to reveal. Breadcrumb back to the season is the first thing in the head, since the only way in is from a card on the board.

Binding. A season is a surface, not a rail. Episodes take the content column — 1124px beside the unchanged 236px production rail — as a grid of four tiles at 257px with a 12px gutter, which is what 30px of side padding leaves. The conversation does not disappear; it moves to one row at the foot, an 850px composer beside the action that turns the season into proposals. This does not widen or replace the 470px rail that turn 44 made binding, and it is not a licence for other views to claim the page: the rail still holds the overview, and Episodes is the single view that earns the surface, because its whole value is comparing episodes to each other. A view you can only see part of is not a board. That is why the rail was tried and refused (45a): it showed five of seven and put the rest under a fold, and a season with its last two episodes below the scroll cannot answer the only question the board exists for — whether episode five earns its place between four and six. Eight tiles fit without scrolling, and the eighth is Add an episode, last in the grid, so making one happens where the others already are. A card carries hook and cliffhanger as two mono lines, the cliffhanger in --warning and a missing ending in --destructive, each stating what it is in words — NO ENDING YET, NO HOOK, NO ENDING — so the colour is never carrying the meaning alone. An unwritten episode is a dashed tile holding a sentence, never an empty slot, the same discipline 43c applies to a seed source with nothing in it: the shape of the season stays honest whether or not it has been written.

Binding. Story is the third instance of the Genesis split, after world Genesis and World Chat, and it is drawn from the same parts: eyebrow-and-h1 head, bubble transcript, a composer carrying attach and voice, and a 470px rail on --muted whose action sits at its foot, full width, size="lg", with a caption beneath. What differs is that a production screen already owns the 236px production rail, so the conversation column is 654px at the 1360px frame rather than the half-page World Chat gets. That is enough because a bubble is capped at 440px regardless, and it is the reason the rail is not widened here: a fourth width would buy the draft nothing and cost the conversation the last of its measure. The rail shows the accepted overview with proposed changes marked on the fields they would change, each carrying the accepted text beneath it — a draft that only showed the new version would make the reader hold the old one in their head. Settledness is carried by the wording (would change, not a rewrite), never by colour alone. Talking writes nothing: every reply carries a receipt ending nothing written, and the single action turns the draft into one proposal for one file — story.json — which is why the label is singular where World Chat’s is plural. Accept stays where it already lives, on the proposals screen. When there is no overview the rail shows dashed cards naming the fields and a third saying the overview may be skipped entirely, because nothing downstream requires one; the action stays visible as variant="outline" with a caption saying why it is not ready, rather than vanishing.

Binding. Creating a production opens that production. The action carries the destination in its label — Create and open day one — because a button that says Create production and then returns to a list has told the user what it made and not where it went, and the list is the one place the thing they just named is hardest to find. Day one is reached by arriving, never by navigating back to it. Day one seeds from two sources, always in this order: open canon threads first, work left uncovered by other productions second. Threads come first because they are the world asking a question, and a production answering one is the thesis; uncovered work is opportunistic and reads as such. Each group carries a heading and a caption naming what it is drawn from, so a group that is empty can say which source is empty rather than disappearing. An empty source renders as a dashed card carrying a sentence (43c), never as a hidden section and never as a generic empty state: a young world is the normal beginning of every world, and a page that goes quiet at the exact moment a person starts is the failure day one exists to prevent. The seed cards are two per row, equal width, and a seed is a single click into drafting with the seed as the brief — it is not a form, and it never dispatches. The dot on a card is --warning for a canon thread and --neutral-400 for uncovered work, and the label beside it names the source record, so the colour is never doing the work alone.

42Small chrome · a permanent way to reach proposals, a cog that looks like a cog, and a face you can see properly

PROPOSALSwhat is waiting on a decision, from every source
ACTIVITYwhat the machine is doing, and what failed
SETTINGSa cog, because it is a cog

Binding. The chrome carries three icons on the right, in the order proposals, activity, settings. Proposals is prepended rather than inserted, because the app’s own chrome records that activity and settings sit "always, in that order" — splitting that pair would reopen a settled decision. Proposals carries the same warning dot as activity when something waits, and reaches the proposals screen from any screen, which is what makes it worth a permanent slot. Settings is a cog; the sliders glyph it replaced reads as filters, and this application has real filter controls that would then wear the same shape. Any reference image opens where it stands — the character’s main photo on its detail page, and both the main photo and the character sheet on the reference page — in an overlay inside the screen rather than a new route, so the page it belongs to stays behind it. The image is zoom-in on hover, the backdrop is zoom-out, and both the backdrop and the close control dismiss it. Navigating away closes it, so it can never be restored underneath a different screen. One discriminator drives all of them rather than a flag per image, so two can never be open at once. The panel is sized to the image’s own aspect, because a dialog whose whole purpose is seeing the picture properly should not letterbox it.

Binding. World Chat is the world’s Genesis: the same split, the same composer, the same rail. Left column flex:1.2 with an eyebrow-and-h1 head, a bubble transcript, and a composer carrying attach and voice; a 470px rail on --muted. The rail’s action sits at its foot, full width, size="lg", with a caption beneath, exactly where Begin in this world sits — it acts on the rail’s contents, so it belongs to the rail. Above that, the world shell: the 44px header with the wordmark centred, the floating nav at top:56px with World Chat active, and content clearing it at 104px. The conversation carries no per-point controls — a point is corrected by talking. Deciding happens exactly twice: wrap-up, and accept. Wrap-up goes straight to the proposals and confirms nothing on the way. There is no preview, because a preview would only summarise the page it is standing in front of. What could not come with the conversation is said on that page, and a choice a proposal still needs is carried on that proposal, where its real values are visible. Creating proposals writes nothing to the world and every one of them can be accepted, sent back or discarded, so the step that needs guarding is Accept, and that is the one that has its own screen. The approvals list column is 265px, and at most one floating layer is open at a time. Below 1100px the split becomes one column: the rail moves beneath the conversation, never over it, so nothing is hidden behind anything else (41c, drawn at 884px against the 1360px desktop frames). That width is where the rail’s 470px stops leaving a conversation column worth reading. The rail keeps its whole contents and loses only its fixed width — there is no drawer, no overlay and no second scroll region. Settledness is carried by the wording, never by colour alone.

Moving pictures has nowhere to go. Seedance 2.0 is still routed here, but it was turned off in Providers. Nothing re-routes on your behalf — pick another model, or turn it back on.

Binding. Availability is per provider, per model, and a model turned off appears in no picker and cannot be a routing default. Defaults are all on, so nothing changes for an existing install. Discovery is a live call, only where a provider offers one — fal publishes a catalogue, Ollama lists what is pulled, OpenAI returns ids without prices, and Higgsfield publishes nothing; a provider that cannot list simply has no button. A discovered model may be enabled only if a price could be read, because an estimate before spending is the whole point of the manifest; anything unpriced is listed and unusable. An enabled-but-undescribed model runs at the floor — referenceImages: 0, no start or end frame, the provider's default size — and is marked unverified everywhere it appears, because understating a capability costs a dropped reference while overstating it costs a dispatch that dies after the estimate was accepted. A routed model that becomes unavailable is stranded: shown, flagged, never silently swapped for another.

Binding. An override is one-shot: it applies to that generation and nothing else. Set as default is the only thing that persists, and it writes to Settings · who does what — there is no third, invisible layer of stickiness. Money is dollars everywhere, never credits; the ledger holds micro-dollars and the figure shown is that number formatted once at the edge. The estimate recomputes from model × count × size on every change, before anything is spent. A resolution a model cannot reach is shown disabled, never hidden, and the same is true of a provider with no key. When the chosen model accepts no reference images, every reference chip it cannot carry must visibly drop — a silent downgrade from image identity to text description is the one failure this surface exists to prevent. The row wraps rather than overflowing or collapsing into a menu: hosts run from 960px to 370px, and the figure, Cancel and the primary button move together as one group so they stay right-aligned on whichever line they land on.

Binding. Art direction is asked during genesis, never inferred from the logline. The step is skippable (Decide later) but not hidden; skipping leaves the world with no look until one is set. A preset seeds the style description and is then discarded — only the text is stored, so an edited preset and a hand-written custom look are the same record. The preset library is identical on both surfaces. Every change to an existing look still goes through the accept gate and takes a new version; earlier work keeps the look it was made under.

35dAppearance tab · three modes, and the one the machine resolved to

appearance · an application preference, never a property of a world
Providers
Appearance
Local runtime
Agents
Who does what
About

THEME
currently using dark
LIGHT
DARK

Binding. Appearance is one application setting, appearance.theme, holding system, light or dark. It lives in %USERPROFILE%/ArkeStudio/settings.json and never in a world, a proposal or the change log — the same world opened on two machines may be read light on one and dark on the other. system is the default and the fallback for any value that fails to parse, and it follows the OS live; an explicit light or dark ignores the OS until the preference returns to system. The resolved theme is applied to the root as .dark, data-theme and color-scheme together, and before the first visible frame — the window stays hidden until the renderer confirms the theme is up, so no launch, reload or update-restart shows a flash of the wrong one. Screens re-theme from semantic tokens only: --muted for a recessed surface, color-mix(in srgb, var(--background) 60%, transparent) for a full-frame wash. Controls and captions drawn over user media use --media-control-* and --media-overlay-*, which are deliberately identical in both themes — the creator's imagery is never recoloured, dimmed or re-framed by the theme.

Binding. Faction cards on 26b are fixed height, and every band in them holds its size whether or not it has content: frame 210; name one clipped 21px line; description a two-line 38px box; wants and fears one clipped 20px line each, always present; links one 20px row that does not wrap, clipping past the third; meta 14. Those band sizes are the contract, not the total. A faction with no fears, or no links, keeps those lines blank rather than shortening its card — the same rule the cast fan follows for an empty role on 1c. Sparse and fully-written factions sit level beside each other, and the card reads as unfinished rather than as a different shape.

Binding. Audio plays through one dock (25c), mounted once for the whole app rather than per screen. Exactly one clip sounds at a time and starting another replaces it. The dock survives navigation — it clears on an explicit dismiss or on closing the world, never on a route change. Every trace of progress — the scrub, the elapsed and total time — lives in the dock alone; a row never draws progress, and a now-playing row changes only its glyph and its --muted tint, holding its geometry exactly. A play affordance is a real button or it is absent: a row whose audio has not been generated shows no circle at all and lets the status dot carry that. The waveform is decorative — seeded from the filename, never from the signal — so it is never a hit target and never a scrub. The dock is min(640px, viewport − 24px) wide; its play control is 30 and its label column 250, both borrowed from the row so the row’s circle reads as becoming the dock’s; the scrub track is 5 high inside a 16 pointer target. It is keyboard-operable within itself — Space toggles, arrows seek — and takes no global hotkey and no volume control, because the system already owns volume.

Binding. Location cards on 23a are fixed height. Every band is pinned — frame 270, name one clipped 20px line, description a two-line 36px box, meta 14 — so the total is a constant at any column width and in every row of the grid. (The band sizes are the contract; the total differs by a pixel or two between this canvas and the app, which wraps the text in its own 2px pad.) Because none of those grow, the meta line sits at the same height on every card; that alignment is the point, not the equal box, which CSS grid would fake within a single row anyway. The description is derived copy — the first sentence of Look — not an authored field, so it is clamped by line and ellipsised at the real break. It is never cut at a character count: a slice at 120 characters lands mid-word and reads as a bug.

Who collects rent in the Drowned Quarter?

I think it's the Ebb Council, quietly. They'd never admit it.
It can work, but it leans on CANON-013: the Council is publicly prudent, privately terrified of the verse. Collecting drowned rent means touching the water they fear. Two ways to hold both: they collect through intermediaries, or the rent collects itself and the Quarter punishes debt. The first needs a name; the second deepens the dread but answers nothing.

The bellkeepers. And nobody has ever seen one collect.
Drafted, the bellkeepers collect for the Council under a name nobody writes down. CANON-013 gains a cross-reference; the Quarter keeps its menace. The entry is on the right.

Can Maren call a tide she has never stood in?
No. CANON-002 is explicit, a caller cannot move a tide she has not stood in, and the song costs hearing with every verse. Maren stood the harbour tide in scene 2 of Saltlight, so the verse rising in scene 4 holds. Open water past the Vigil is outside her reach until she stands in it, and each call she makes costs her another verse of hearing.

NEW WORLD

Start talking. It starts existing.

A coastal city where a drowned god still sings, and some people can hear it.
Then the city has learned to live around the song, bells muffled, harbours rebuilt twice. I've called it The Undersong for now; one word from you changes it. Who hears the song first: someone who profits from it, someone haunted by it, or someone whose job it is?
seeded: title · logline · tone (quiet dread) · all proposed, nothing locked
Whose job it is. A tide-caller, the last one. She's paid to move water, but she hears the verse underneath it.
A working woman, not a chosen one, that keeps the dread quiet. I've sketched her as Maren Kest, and given the harbour a counterweight: the Vigil, a lighthouse whose keeper listens for what shouldn't answer back. Two threads I've left open on the right. Pull either one when you're ready.

6s · 2.39:1 · seed 4417 Cancel Dispatch

Binding. World cards on 1a are fixed height, and the dashed New world card is the same height — both take it from one declaration so they cannot drift apart. Bands: key art 256×286, name one clipped 24px line, logline a two-line 39px box, meta one 15px line. Nothing here stretches — the row is laid out align-items:flex-start, so each card is exactly its own content and a logline that grows from a sentence to a paragraph takes the card with it. A world with no logline still renders the box, empty, or its card comes up short. And the counts in the meta line are their own clipped element: left as a bare text node they form an anonymous flex item that wraps internally, which turns a 15px band into 38px as soon as the timestamp is longer than 2h ago.

Binding. The cast fan on 1c is a grid of fixed cards: every polaroid is 170px wide with a 180px frame, a name of one 17px line and a role of one 15px line. Both text lines clip with an ellipsis rather than wrap, so no card grows to fit its copy and height is a constant rather than a function of content. A character's role is capped at 28 characters — the width budget of that 147px line at 11px in the sans face, measured at the average letter density of the roles drawn here, every one of which fits: Tide-caller (11), Cartographer (12), Salvage diver (13), Warden of the Vigil (19), What the deep sends up (22). The cap is a budget for authoring, not a guarantee — 28 wide capitals would still overrun — so the clip stays as the backstop, and the cap binds only where a role is written: a world already holding a longer one still opens, clipped. An empty role stays empty. The card never substitutes prose from the sheet body; a character with no role shows a blank line that keeps its 15px, so the card reads as unfinished rather than as a wall of essence text, and the fan stays level either way.

Binding. A sheet’s Essence is its lead paragraph, and the actions on it sit in a footer row beneath that paragraph (3a) — never beside a heading, where they compete with the section name and jump as the copy reflows. The row is 26×22 ghost icon buttons at gap:2, pulled -6px left so the first glyph optically aligns with the text above it, 10px under the paragraph. It is not shown until the text is under the pointer (or something in it holds focus), and it hides with opacity and pointer-events, never display — the row keeps its box at all times, so revealing it moves nothing on the page. While its clip is the loaded one the row stays visible with the pointer gone, since a tint nobody can see cannot say where the sound came from. Read aloud is a speaker, never a play triangle: it starts the read and hands transport to the dock (25c), so it never becomes a pause and never grows a scrub — while its clip is the one loaded it takes the --accent active tint, so the sound can be traced back to the text that made it. Copy takes the paragraph as plain text. A read that will be charged states its cost in this same row, the icons giving way to the character count and price until it is confirmed or dismissed; a read that failed reports beneath the row, never in the heading.

Binding. The voice picker (3b) is a list, not a ranking. It opens straight onto the catalogue — no matching step to press through first — and it never scores a voice against the sheet: no percentage, no matched to, no re-match action. A voice is judged by hearing it, which is what the previews are for; a number beside a name only invites arguing with the number. Each row states the voice’s own attributes rather than which of them overlapped the writing. The highlighted row is the one currently assigned to this character, marked current; where none is assigned, nothing is highlighted.
